That the Government of Canada provide some leadership by finding ways and means of keeping the cost of production down by increasing the returns to producers and by eliminating unnecessary costs, tariffs and taxes before the industry is completely destroyed.

According to recent figures from Statistics Canada, what a dollar would buy in the way of groceries in 1971 now costs the Canadian consumer $2.85. That the heartless, do-nothing Minister of Finance inform this House of the immediate measures he intends to take to assist Canadians who are finding it increasingly difficult to feed their families.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF FULL-TIME MINISTER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Today, more than ever, veterans deserve better treatment from the government. They are now faced with an inflation rate of 12.4 per cent, an increase in gas prices of 52 cents per gallon, heating oil increases of $1.12 per gallon, food cost hikes of 15.2 per cent, and a do-nothing budget. On top of all this they are being administered by a department which is receiving no leadership and is taking up to two years to process their pension applications. There is also the fact that some veterans are dying before they receive their pensions. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to appoint a full-time Minister of Veterans Affairs immediately and that this new minister launch a full-fledged investigation into the totally unacceptable conditions in the Department of Veterans Affairs.

projects, with a more realistic National Energy Program in place, would improve the investment climate in Canada and relieve the pressure on our dollar, which is currently producing record high interest rates, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House condemn the Minister of Finance for his repeated stonewalling of the Canadian public and demand that he produce a new budget and energy program and, if he is not capable of doing so, that he tender his resignation immediately.

subsubtopic: LOW COST LOANS FOR MUNICIPALITIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, interest rates which affect the cost of capital borrowing by municipalities across this country are a matter of urgent and pressing necessity because they increase the property taxes of every Canadian. In the Ottawa-Carleton regional area, for example, only one and a half months ago the executive committee was talking about a borrowing rate of 14'/2 per cent for their capital necessities. Today the rate is over 16 per cent. Therefore it will cost three and a half times as much by the time they pay back the debt. Winnipeg is another example. Under present interest rates, the average householder will have to pay $30 to carry the capital costs of local public works. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government immediately implement a program of low-cost loans for capital purposes to municipalities.

I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance and ask him to comment about the real growth we are seeing in our chartered banks whose profits have risen to a quarter of the total profits of all the public companies in Canada, up 66 per cent compared to the same quarter last year, due to the high interest rate structure favoured by the minister. Would the Minister of Finance explain to the House why he chooses to favour a policy which is obviously so beneficial to our chartered banks at a time when countless numbers of small businesses are going bankrupt as a result of it?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think 1 should remind hon. members opposite, who have properly raised the plight of the small business firms, that we have in operation the small business development bond which has been extended by this government and which brings very substantial interest rate benefit to eligible small businesses in the country. So, we have responded in these inflationary times to the requests which were made to us by the small business representatives in continuing the small business development bond.
The hon. member has mentioned the profitability of the banks. It is true that for one quarter, and possibly two quarters, there is a strong improvement in the profitability of the banks, stemming from a rather low base. I have already indicated to members of the House of Commons on previous occasions that it is my intention to monitor the situation very closely, since I do not believe that any particular institution in the country should be permitted to benefit in any unfair or inequitable way from the current high interest rates which are necessary for the welfare of the Canadian economy.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:

The inflation level has gone up a full 4 per cent since he introduced this policy and, oddly enough, the prime lending rates have gone up 4.5 per cent. Would the minister explain to the House when we will be entering this promised land he told us he was leading us to-a

promised land with lower inflation, which would be the fallout of his following a high interest rate policy? We certainly have the high interest rates but, unfortunately, we have even higher inflation. When will we get to the point where there is lower inflation in the country? speechtext: 1 wish to ask a supplementary question, Madam Speaker. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are trying to understand what the Minister of Finance just obfuscated. Since the mid-1960s the standard term for a mortgage has been five years. We now have one and two-year mortgages, and there is some talk even of six-month mortgages. subtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON MORTGAGE MARKET

Madam Speaker, I have a good many concerns and one of those concerns is obviously the impact of the very high interest rates on home owners and other groups in the community. My overriding concern is the very strong inflation that we are experiencing at the present time in Canada and my corollary that the present interest rates are absolutely essential if we are going to make any possible headway against inflation. That is the simple proposition that has to be admitted.
If hon. members ask me, as they are doing, either to protect every group in the country by new spending, or many groups in the country by new spending, or by taking a deliberate action to lower interest rates in current circumstances, they are asking me to do something that I will not do, namely, to take steps that would add further to inflation in the long term. They are saying, "lower it now," and I am telling them that if 1 did that they would get it in spades in the long term.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF COST OF LIVING TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have had it in clubs from the minister today. Four months ago he was blaming the Americans, something he has done again today, and last week he was blaming the Canadian worker for the kind of inflation we have been suffering. Instead of blaming the Canadian worker whose wages have fallen behind the rise in the cost of living in the past four years, and in view of
the effect this has on people on fixed incomes or pensions, why does the minister continue to reject a cost of living tax credit which is not a blanket subsidy but would be a method of using the tax system to provide the kind of protection and help that those Canadians trying to keep up with increases in the cost of living so desperately need, and which would focus that assistance on people who need it most?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance

I attempted to mention, in a speech in Toronto, how inflationary expectations in the current strong inflationary environment have fed through into wage settlements which, in my view, will lead in the long term to no benefit for individual workers, or for the economy. That is what I have been saying. If the hon. member can show how I am wrong on that, I would be glad to hear him.
The hon. member is asking me to provide protection through a tax credit for a special group in the community. That is what he is doing. He is not arguing that it is costless. He is not saying that it will not cost the treasury anything. It is obviously going to cost money. It is is going to add to spending. It is going to add to the deficit or add to higher taxes, both of which, in these circumstances, would be unacceptable as far as I am concerned.

Madam Speaker, the minister's commitment to social Darwinism would be quaint were its effect on the average Canadian not so devastating. If he sticks around tomorrow and Thursday, he will hear from us how the economy can afford to pay for a cost of living tax credit by putting taxes on the banks and taxing our largest corporations at a rate which the average taxpayer also pays. The money is there if the minister is prepared to find it.
My supplementary question to the minister is this, Madam Speaker. When the Bank of Canada started its policy of gradualism in 1975, we had an inflation rate of 10 per cent and an interest rate of 9.75 per cent. Now we have inflation running at an annual rate of nearly 14 per cent and interest rates running at 20 per cent. By what empirical test does the minister have to be convinced that the policy which the bank has been following, on his instructions and on the instructions of the hon. member for St. John's West-under what conditions does the minister have to say that this policy clearly is not working and we have to find an alternative that will have the effect of reducing inflation without killing the Canadian economy and without hurting the average Canadian?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the highest interest rates and cost of living ever recorded in Canadian history, which have caused economic ruin for thousands of Canadians, particularly home owners, farmers, small businessmen and fishermen; and the necessity for the government to institute a new made-in-Canada interest rate policy that will stop fuelling inflation and the resulting hardship for the ordinary Canadian.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) gave me notice of his intention to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of debating certain aspects of the economic conditions of the country, more particularly interest rates.
The hon. member will know that in arriving at a decision on such a motion the Chair must be guided by the provisions of subsection (5) of the Standing Order, which in part reads as follows:
In determining whether a matter should have urgent consideration. Madam Speaker... shall have regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means.
As early as tomorrow and the day following, opposition motions may be set down for debate in the House under supply proceedings if hon. members so choose.
Members will recall the lengthy debate which was allowed by the Chair under the same Standing Order on December 18 and 19 last dealing with economic conditions in Canada, a subject quite similar to that which the hon. member asks be debated today. It is obvious that the Chair under these conditions and on this matter, which is of a continuing nature, cannot accept the hon. member's request for an emergency debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

speechtext:
1. Yes. "The Buffalo Shuffle" is a colloquial phrase
May 12, 1981

often applied to a commission procedure, facilitating admission for humanitarian or compassionate reasons of people already in Canada, but who are subject to a deportation, removal, or exclusion order and are required by law to leave the country. The same procedure may also be applied to those whose admission is deemed to be in the national interest, such as some entrepreneurs. Many such people seeking admission by this procedure are from the Toronto area, and are referred for processing to the Canadian consulate in Buffalo because of its proximity to the border; hence the phrase "Buffalo Shuffle." This phrase is sometimes also applied to the same procedure used at other Canadian consulates in the U.S.A. At the consulate's own discretion or at the request of immigration officials at national or regional headquarters, ministerial permits are issued to persons who meet the foregoing requirements, but whose admission to Canada is otherwise prohibited by law. Another large group to whom the term "Buffalo Shuffle" may be applied are individuals legally in Canada in the visitors category who are applying to remain as permanent residents through a Canadian consulate in the U.S.A.

Statistics Canada reports: 1. Data on deaths due to unnatural causes are collected through two different statistical programs: the vital statistics program which gathers information based on reports from death certificates provided by provincial registrars, and the homicide statistics program which gathers basic information provided by police forces across Canada. The figures from the two programs differ for two reasons: they are collected by two different means and use different definitions. According to the homicide program, homicide is defined such that it includes all suspected cases of criminal homicide (murder, manslaughter and infanticide) occurring in Canada, regardless of whether a suspect has been identified in the killing. The program does not include Canadian residents killed in other countries. The vital statistics program makes no reference to the legal terms murder, manslaughter or infanticide. Rather, deaths are classified as having been caused by injuries inflicted by another person with intent to injure and kill, by any means. The latest data available from the vital statistics program, the 1979 preliminary death statistics, are as follows:
Total deaths by unnatural causes 16,556 (Includes deaths caused by environmental events, circumstances and conditions.)
Total deaths by suicide and self-inflicted injury 3,357
Deaths by suicide and self-inflicted injury resulting from use of firearms 1,085
Total deaths by homicide and injury purposefully inflicted by other persons 583 (Includes injuries inflicted by another person with intent to injure or kill, by any means. Excludes injuries on account of legal intervention and operations of war.)

The equivalent figures for 1980 are not yet available, however preliminary figures for the first nine months of 1980 show that 15 per cent fewer homicide offences were committed than during the same period in 1979. Over the past decade the percentage of homicides committed with firearms has declined from a high of 47 per cent in 1974 to 33 per cent in 1979.

The House resumed from Wednesday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on second reading of this important bill, which is the first major social justice bill to come before this House in over three decades, I must say I am sorry the minister in whose name the bill stands and who will have a

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
great deal to do with its administration and negotiations with the provinces, is not present in the House this afternoon. This minister will also have a great deal to do with the bill once it has reached committee. I find his absence not only surprising but quite appalling, particularly as the minister and the government seemed to be in such a rush just prior to the Easter Irecess to pull a fast one, at least in the minds of many of us, by introducing this bill at a time when he knew the justice committee was sitting on other important legislation and, to the minister's knowledge, I was away from Ottawa with some of the minister's own colleagues. As I say, I am terribly surprised he is not here this afternoon in the House to listen to the debate on this very important measure.
In speaking about the debate which took place on April 15 last, I find myself in a little bit of a predicament. There were at least four members who spoke on that afternoon who I thought did an exceptionally good job in describing some of the complex provisions of the bill and some of its implications once it goes through the House. I do not say when this bill goes through the House, or if it goes through; I say once it goes through the House, because our position in this party I am sure is crystal clear as a result of those four speeches on April 15. lam sure it is crystal clear to the government, and I hope it is clear to the people of this country that we are wholeheartedly in support of its concept.
I thought the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn), who led off for this side, did an exceedingly able job of outlining the various parts of the bill. He took a bird's eye view of the legislation; he took an overview of it. I felt, quite frankly, because of such short notice, and especially in view of the rather tricky nature in which the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) introduced the bill, indicating he thought it should go through with one or two speeches-obviously it should not- the hon. member for Saskatoon West did a very admirable job. He did such a good job I am not left with much scope this afternoon.
I thought the speech by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) was particularly useful to this House from the point of view of a person who has dealt in a very practical way in the courts of this country with the problems emanating from the existing legislation.
I thought the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) added a great deal as a non-lawyer. Then my good friend and able lawyer, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), finished up that day's debate in a very admirable way.
I have just a few small points to make and I will not be too long. Firstly, I find it almost inexcusable that the Liberal government of the day has delayed in bringing this legislation forward. I would like to just quote one fatuous and to my mind inexcusable comment by the Solicitor General when he opened the debate on April 15 in this House in my absence. He said this:
Because of the large number of solicitors general of Canada in the last five or six years, possibly none of them has been in a position to review the provisions and bring forward a bill which they would have been prepared to explain, defend and discuss with the provinces in the final sense.
I do not know whether the Solicitor General was speaking of his own party colleagues who had been his predecessors in the office of the solicitor general, and perhaps he was, but I am fair-minded enough to think that all of the solicitors general in this country in the last decade had a fair hand in helping to prepare this legislation. The position we arrive at today is that this legislation is almost exactly the same as the legislation I as the solicitor general put forward to the provinces and tabled in this House in the fall of 1979.
Indeed, as I go through the bill in a detailed way I find it is exactly the same as the Conservative government proposal in the fall of 1979, with only one major exception and a few minor ones. The minor exceptions are really very technical in nature and, I must say, in my mind, increase the efficiency of the bill, representing an improvement. They relate to some very minor technical details and wording in relation to the privacy of proceedings, the review of dispositions and, finally, the availability of the records of juvenile offenders. Those are the only variances with the proposal put forward by the Clark administration in the fall of 1979, with one other major exception which I will come to later.
Therefore, I find it quite exceptional, almost insulting, to have the solicitor general of this day, speaking in his opening statement in this House in respect of this first major piece of social justice legislation in three decades, attempt to take the partisan attitude he did, casting aspersions not only on me as a predecessor in that office but also on his own colleagues on his side of the House who were also his predecessors in that office.
The fact remains that the bill before the House now, Bill C-61, to all intents and purposes is the bill I had prepared in the office of the solicitor general during the summer of 1979 when I was there. I might add that I took great pains to push and give high priority to that bill to make sure the House of Commons of the day was brought up to date with what was happening, and especially to make sure that at every stage in the drafting of the bill the provinces, which are so much involved with the implications arising from this measure, and upon whom a great deal of the burden will inevitably fall, were kept informed. Certainly the bill I had prepared and the bill which has been presented by the present Solicitor General are almost exactly word for word, except for one major point. That one major point is one that to my mind represents a fatal flaw in this bill, as I have described it before.
With the permission of the Chair I hope to do something today which might correct that one fatal flaw. There are two points I want to make, and I will be very brief. The first point is that this bill will require full and complete discussion in the committee by everyone in this House who is involved with, and interested in, criminal justice in this country. But especially there must be a full opportunity in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for provincial representatives to come with their suggestions and criticisms.
I know that one of the excuses of the government may be that negotiations and discussions with the provinces have been
May 12, 1981

going on for almost a decade in relation to this reforming piece of legislation. That is true. Those discussions and negotiations have been going on, but the House should fully appreciate that this bill has implications for the provinces, for the administration of justice in the provinces and for the provincial treasuries far more than it does for the federal government, any federal government agency and, indeed, the federal treasury.
I think it will be essential that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs of this House make sure that the provinces have a full and ample opportunity to make their cases, because they do have cases to make. There are differences. There are differing cases to make, but I think this House owes something to the people of this country, to the young people of the future who will come into conflict with the law and especially to the taxpayers of this country for whom this bill will have very great implications. There certainly must be full, ample and open opportunity for the provincial governments to come to that committee as well as-and I say this just as an obvious argument, which I am sure 1 do not have to make-the many semi-public and private agencies which deal with young offenders and young people in the life of this country. I hope they also have a full opportunity to come before that committee.
However, in spite of the negotiations the provincial representatives should be able to come to that committee to make their representations, because the financial implications of this bill are such that 1 am not too sure that the staff of the present minister really knows or understands some of those financial implications for the provinces involved.
What will be the situation, for instance, under the Canada Assistance Plan with respect to payments in relation to youthful offenders, in relation to child welfare or in relation to young people in Canada? Here in Ottawa through the Department of National Health and Welfare we are very easily able to obtain information on the total payments to the provinces for child welfare, which includes youthful offenders, amounting to almost $80 million in 1978-79. I find it very surprising that apparently nowhere in the Department of National Health and Welfare-nowhere in the federal bureaucracy, in any event, that we have been able to discover-can we yet learn just what percentage of that $80 million for 1978-79 was devoted to young people who came into conflict with the criminal law. Yet obviously a good percentage of that money was paid out through provincial administrations and down through the myriad of bureaucratic agencies at the provincial level for child welfare and for young people in Canada who have come into conflict with the criminal law. I stress again that $80 million per year. I suspect that the amount paid in transfer payments by the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan to the provinces is higher now than $80 million per year.
Those payments will be vitally affected, obviously, by this legislation because the whole concept will be changed, and I hope somewhere along the line, if and when we receive a reply from any meaningful person on the government benches, we will learn these figures and exactly how much has been paid
Young Offenders Act
out, say, in the last ten years in relation to child welfare payments to the provinces under the CAP. I hope we will find out how those payments will be affected by this legislation. If the minister, the parliamentary secretary and their staff have done their homework, then obviously they will have those figures at their fingertips and will be able to give them to us.
There is another area of grave financial concern with respect both to the federal treasury and the provincial treasuries. I am sure Your Honour is aware that currently there are young offenders' special agreements with four of the provinces of this country. Between the federal Department of National Health and Welfare and the provincial governments there have been four agreements worked out over the years dealing with young offenders. There are federal government transfer payments under those agreements to the provinces to assist them in the administration of this important work.
Just in the last three years alone, for instance, New Brunswick has received $1.5 million. In just two years Yukon has received three quarters of a million dollars. In one year Quebec-and this is a partial payment only relating back over a number of years, to 1974-received over $38 million. My own home province of Ontario in just the last three years alone has received over $50 million in payments from the federal government in relation to young offenders. Again I mention these figures only to emphasize some of the financial implications-and only some of the financial implications-for the federal treasury and the provincial treasuries in relation to this particular legislation.
This is no two-bit, picayune piece of legislation. This bill is important from a social justice and social welfare point of view, and it is extremely important as well in relation to administrative and transfer costs between the federal government and the provincial governments.
Another area to which I do not think enough attention has been given by the current minister in respect of provincial cost is the whole question of provincial legal aid, which is paid for and administered by the provinces. This bill has as one of its minor-major-if I can put it in that fashion-provisions the right of young offenders to counsel. This is something which has not been detailed for them before. This is an important section of the bill. The right of young offenders to counsel is not a privilege; they have a right to be represented before the courts by counsel.
Quite frankly, I was surprised that in outlining his position in relation to this bill the minister did not deal with this, but I would like to have some idea of how this will affect the various provincial legal aid funds and the administration of legal aid across the country. Has this section and its implications for the provincial treasuries been outlined to the provinces? Do the provinces know what the federal government is getting them into in relation to this important, but necessary, piece of legislation? I do not know. We do not know because the minister has not seen fit to tell us if he knows or not, and if he knows, just what he does know.
The final point I want to make is with respect to the major fatal flaw in this legislation. As I have said, in all important

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
respects this bill is the same as the bill prepared and made ready for introduction by the Clark administration for the winter of 1980. Indeed, it was going to be introduced, to the knowledge of the provincial governments and this House- because we said so in the fall of 1979-in the winter of 1980, if we had remained in office, except for one section, and that one section is integral to the whole bill.
The concept of this legislation is that it is a reforming piece of legislation which will be the reference piece of legislation for young people when they run afoul of the criminal law. The concept of it has to be built into what the definition of a young offender actually is, and this changes the whole set-up. Instead of varying ages across the country with the patchwork, crazy quilt-like situation that we have at the moment, in my mind I was pushing this particular bill in 1979 because the major reforming essence of the bill had to be that we wanted uniformity in the definition of what a young offender was across this country, whether in Cape Breton Island or Vancouver Island.
It is obviously essential, when you are dealing with criminal justice, that there be uniformity across this country. Otherwise, there is no reason for the federal government to be involved with criminal law, especially when the administration of criminal law is basically a provincial concern. Obviously, criminal law in this country has to be uniform. People have to be equal in the sight and in the eyes of justice when they come before the courts of this land.
One of the major defects in the system at the moment in respect of juvenile delinquents, in respect of young people when they run afoul of the criminal law, is that they are not treated equally across this country. Mr. Speaker, I bring this to your attention because I know that as a member of Parliament from the Ottawa area you have bumped into this in your constituency work. Someone aged 17 who under exactly the same circumstances commits an offence at one end of the Hull-Ottawa bridge will be treated quite differently in the eyes of the law and before the courts of the land from one who commits the same offence at the other end of the Hull-Ottawa bridge, simply because age makes a difference in the various pieces of provincial legislation which exist across this country.
At the moment, for instance, these differences exist; in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba the maximum age of a juvenile delinquent, a young person who runs afoul of the law, is a person under 18 years. In other words, 18 is the maximum age for a youthful offender in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba. In the province of British Columbia, the maximum age is under 17 years. In Newfoundland, where the Juvenile Deliquents Act is not applied but they have their own provincial statute, under their legislation the maximum age is 16 and one half years. In all the remaining provinces and territories the age is under 16 years.
Quite frankly, I had some tactical reasons for introducing the provision that I did when I was solicitor general under the Clark administration. Most of the provinces provide that the
maximum age for a youthful offender is a person under 16 years. The majority of the provinces agree that that should be indicated as the uniform age across this country in the new legislation. That was not my doing; that was the doing of my predecessors, and I give them full credit for it. But somebody had to grasp the nettle. Someone had to come up with a uniform age. Otherwise, in my mind, the whole purpose and reason for this reforming legislation would fall to the ground.
I therefore picked 16 years as the maximum age in the legislation that I proposed in 1979. My tactical reasons for doing so were simply that that was the view of the majority of the provinces, and if in the public debate that would take place in this House and in the committee compelling and forthright reasons were put forward by those few provinces that opposed that view in a way in which public opinion and the members of this House could be swayed, then certainly we in the federal government could retreat somewhat by arriving at the compromise of 17 years. If the worst came to the worst, I was even prepared to go to 18 years. But I really did not care whether it was 16, 17 or 18 years.
The age of majority in this country, in any event, is an accident of history. There is no logic or sense behind 21, 35, 18 or 16 years in most of our statutory provisions across this country, in any event. They are usually not based on technical or scientific data. They are just stabs in the dark or grabs out of a hat. I did not care whether it was 16, 17 or 18. I will be honest with you, Mr. Speaker, I do not care to this day. But what I do care about is that all people in this country be equal in the eyes of the law. That is the fundamental principle behind this legislation, and that is why I wanted to see a uniform age.
The present Solicitor General, on his own-

I think he has fundamentally changed the concept that I was prepared to bring in in 1979, because he says that 18 is the age unless any of the provinces opt out. We have heard quite a bit about what a damaging and deleterious concept it is to permit provincial governments to opt out of important legislation in this country, and yet here we have the government and the Solicitor General doing just exactly that.

That is a fatuous, almost inconceivable concept, in my mind, and it destroys the fundamental essence and basis of this reforming legislation, which is to require that people are equal in the eyes of the criminal courts and the criminal law of this country, and this will continue. To my mind, the definition section is a fatal flaw, a fatal error, in this legislation. I cannot speak with any more emotion or passion or, I hope, logic in my arguments to try to convince this House that this is a fatal flaw in the legislation and that it should be changed.
May 12, 1981

I know that there are grave problems with introducing amendments on second reading in this House. It has only been accomplished once or twice before in the eight or nine years that I have been here, and one of those times I was able to do it; but it has only been done once or twice, I believe. I think that what the Solicitor General has done is destroy the essence and the main principle of this legislation, which has to be that in criminal law all people are equal in the sight of the law and in the way they are treated by that law.
I think that is a very important principle, Sir, and you do not have to take only my word for it. Very many private agencies which have studied this bill over the last few months are taking the same view. As for the provincial Bar associations, the last item to cross my desk indicated that the Manitoba Bar is taking similar points of view, that this is excellent reforming legislation except that the Solicitor General has chickened out. He has copped out. He has opted out in respect of the maximum age.
1 think this question is important enough to the very essence and principle of this bill that I am now prepared to move what I would like Your Honour to accept as a reasoned amendment with respect to this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the Young Offenders Act and the way in which we treat our young people who come into conflict with our criminal justice system. As a preface to my remarks, and as the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) will know, our spokesman on this bill, the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), has already indicated the feelings of our party with respect to this legislation.
If the primary thrust of this legislation is to distinguish between someone called a "young offender" and everyone else under the Criminal Code, and if the Young Offenders Act will apply to a specific group of people and the Criminal Code to another, then it is elementary and quite fundamental that the act must contain a consistent definition of "young offender". I applaud the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland for his attack on a patchwork quilt notion of rights in Canada. I
Young Offenders Act
welcome him to our side. In my view, if the Supreme Court rules in a particular way, and if we do have a charter of rights as a result of the resolution of this House, then the failure of the act to define the concept of a young offender and the fact that someone may be subject to the Criminal Code in Ontario and not subject to it in Manitoba is clearly in breach of Section 15 of the charter. The charter makes it very clear that discrimination on the basis of age will not be allowed.
If we accept the fact that the federal government has a responsibility to define the meaning of "young offender" and the difference between someone who will be subject to the Criminal Code and someone who will not be subject to it, then it would seem to me that the making of laws with respect to criminal justice is specifically and explicitly under the jurisdiction of the federal government. I submit that all parties must accept that because it is part of the British North America Act. Even without a charter of rights I think it can well be argued-and I have personally felt this for a long time-that an anomalous definition of "juvenile delinquent" is in itself a problem with respect to our existing Constitution.
I want to spend a few moments attempting to describe for the House, as I understand it, what we are talking about here. Prior to 1908 there was, and there continues to be, a variety of child welfare acts throughout the provinces which deal with the problems of children who are deemed by their communities to be in need of control of some kind, apart from parental or familial control. The general rule is that the provisions of the Criminal Code apply to offences against it which have been committed by people regardless of their age. If one looks back to common law cases in the seventeenth, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it will be found that there were very unhappy experiences taking place. At that time the situation existed where children aged ten and 11 were actually hanged for stealing. The history of the criminal justice system is filled with examples of incredible injustices being done to children well below the age of responsibility and maturity. These children were punished in incredibly harsh terms under the full force of the Criminal Code because they had either committed an offence against the Criminal Code or against the common law.
At the beginning of the twentieth century there was a movement of reform which was not unique to Canada but in which Canada took part. That reform professed that we must protect children and provide a unique system of laws and a unique system of justice for them. The reform provided that children should be treated differently because they are children and because they cannot be deemed to be responsible for their actions. The concept of taking responsibility for one's actions is at the very heart of the criminal justice system in our society. The notion of responsibility and punishment only makes sense in the context of one being responsible for one's actions. That is part of the moral fibre of our system of criminal justice.
The Juvenile Delinquents Act was passed in 1908. Amendments subsequent to 1908 had a number of problems associated with them. In substituting a paternal or maternal regime

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
for the notion of criminal responsibility, we took away some rights. Obviously rights and responsibilities go together. In a sense we substituted the beneficent state for the responsible child.
In doing so I think we did some good things and some bad things. On the good side we obviously advanced the interests of children. We kept children out of the criminal justice system until it was absolutely unavoidable on account of age. But there are problems associated with having done that, the most important of which being that the Juvenile Delinquents Act provides categories of offences which are called status offences. In other words, it matters not what you have done but who you are.
I think this concept has been expressed by members of all parties. If the juvenile court decides that a child is a juvenile delinquent because of his behaviour, social position, the crowd he hangs around with, or because vandalism has been occurring in an area that he has frequented, the court does not have to be satisfied that the child has, in fact, committed an offence; the court can decide that because the child has been hanging around when he should have been at home, he is a juvenile offender and in need of punishment of some kind or another. The concept of status offences of this kind is clearly offensive to us. It takes away from the rights of children who, after all, are just little people. It takes away from the notion of responsibility which, as I say, is the essence of the criminal justice system as it has been established.
I must say, however, that that was not the only problem which was part and parcel of the Juvenile Delinquency Act. There were many problems associated with the administration of justice and with the responsibility of the provinces which I will not get into. There were problems of detention, problems of the kind of care which you relinquish a subject to, problems of the general decline of respect for the system which all parties to the system began to feel. There were the problems that are inevitably associated with a machinery and a philosophy which was clearly out of date and unable to deal with the explosion of juvenile crime which we are witnessing in our cities today.
There are other technical problems which are of some importance and with which, it seems to me, an act would want to deal. One technical problem is what you do in the instance where someone designated by a province to be a juvenile commits or is alleged to commit an offence together with someone who is not a juvenile. In that instance you have the anomalous situation where a juvenile could be involved in a crime, which could be one of some seriousness, and would be charged and tried on the basis of the juvenile delinquency system, while the partner in the offence would be tried in accordance with the Criminal Code. I know of instances where the partner who was tried in accordance with the Criminal Code was found not guilty because the state was unable to prove its case, but the juvenile was declared to be a juvenile delinquent and was detained because the burden of proof and
the rights of the accused are so different within the juvenile system and the criminal system.
There is, of course, the right granted under the Juvenile Delinquency Act for a judge to order that a case be transferred from the juvenile court to the mainstream of the criminal justice system. Indeed, that is now the general rule rather than the exception. There are many cases of 16 and 17-year-olds being taken out of the juvenile system and put into the mainstream of the criminal system just because the judge- and one could understand the reasoning behind this-said that he did not want to see an anomaly created where one person was convicted for participating in an offence while the other person was let go, even though they had both been involved.
The problem with that is that we are then, in a sense, offending the very purpose for which we established a separate juvenile delinquency system in 1908. We are saying that we accept, for the purposes of this particular act and this particular crime, because it happened to be committed with an older person, that this young person has the prerequisite sense of responsibility and the prerequisite liability to punishment. In my opinion, the problem of transfers is a fundamental one and any new bill should deal with it.
The concerns of our party have been set out very well by the hon. member for Burnaby. I want to reinforce them and to indicate that we will put forward some amendments in committee and will be having discussion there where we will expect the minister to explain the position he has put forward.
Our specific concerns are, first of all, that if we are going to have a separate system, which we all agree we should have, let us not take anything away from the positive thrust of the reforms of 1908. As the hon. member for Burnaby said, let us not go overboard toward simply writing a Criminal Code for young people under the aegis of a fiction that you can ascribe the same degree of responsibility for what are called crimes to a young person as you can to someone who has reached the age of majority. In my view there is a danger that this is, in fact, what has been done.
The declaration of principle set out in clause 3 of the bill reads as follows:
(a) while young persons should not in all instances be held accountable in the same manner or suffer the same consequences for their behaviour as adults, young persons who commit offences should nonetheless bear responsibility for their contraventions and society must be afforded the necessary protection from illegal behaviour-
I am very concerned that in a declaration of principles for the Young Offenders Act, which is a departure for this Parliament and for Canada, we fail to specify very clearly that we are also very much concerned with the welfare of the young person; that the rehabilitation of the young person is the primary object of the exercise. If we want to preserve the rights of young people when they come into conflict with the law-I will have something to say about where the Young Offenders Act falls down in that regard-we should not provide that a ten-year-old or an eight-year-old or a 13-year-old who has committed a crime should be treated as if he were as responsible as a 20-year-old. We should not be silent in the
May 12, 1981

declaration of principle on the question of the primary objective of any system dealing with young people. It would be a mistake not to say that the Canadian people are concerned about ensuring that a ten-year-old is not forever held responsible and treated in the same way as a 20 or 30-year-old, or that rehabilitation is the primary objective. I believe that there is in the criminal justice system itself the notion-which is endemic to our whole system of values, our whole concept of freedom, and which we get from our religious backgrounds- that while there is life there is hope and the means of redemption, if you like, speaking in religious terms; or simply that the individual has the means to change or to erase or atone for a mistake. That should be at the very heart of our criminal justice system.
Even more should that same concept or notion be attached to the acts of a 12 or 14-year-old. They should be able to say that they are sorry, that they made a terrible mistake and would like to reform and be rehabilitated. It seems to me a major error that that notion is not in the declaration of principle. In my opinion, the notion that a young person is in all circumstances as responsible as an older person is a fiction, and it should be treated as such. It is an important fiction, because the notion that we are responsible individuals, free to choose whether we will commit wrong, is what makes the punishment system work. It is what makes our concept of rights so important. It is the notion of individuals having responsibility that makes the concept of human rights so important in our protection of that responsibility.
I want to turn next to the question of rights. The bill makes important advances. It does give certain rights. It does provide the right to counsel and the right to bail and it provides some very important rights with respect to sentencing. It does take away from the general paternal discretion which, as I said, was endemic or part and parcel of the do-gooding state notion which was part of the 1908 reform. [DOT]
We have gone back on that in this act because we have something called alternative measures. Alternative measures are what the technocrats in this field call diversion. These are set out in Section 4 of the act. What diversion and what alternative measures really mean is that in certain circumstances, as soon as the kid is caught and charged, it is possible that he or she will never see the inside of a youth court. All of us might say that is a good thing. I say that is a good thing, but I question how one gets to be subject to what are called alternative measures. The idea is that you say to the child, "Look, rather than go through all this system, how would you like to engage in a form of alternative service? How would you like to be subject to a certain kind of parole regime or how would you like to be taken away from your parents"-or whatever alternative arrangement is made-"and placed under the jurisdiction of the youth court?" In other words, we will give the offender that alternative rather than having to plead guilty or not guilty.
Young Offenders Act
As the hon. member for Burnaby has said, the problem is that there must be some kind of screening mechanism which protects the child and allows the child to say that he wants to plead not guilty. This is allowed in this document. It is notionally voluntary and it is notionally restricted. The concept of innocence does not exist in our criminal justice system. We have no such thing as innocence. One is simply guilty or not guilty. If a child wants to exercise his or her right to do that, it seems to me that we have to safeguard that right more than we have done as provided by the alternative measures notion.
This problem of diversion has been discussed at some length by my colleague from Burnaby and I do not want to go into it at any greater length except to say that you cannot grant rights on the one hand, and then provide for the same kind of paternalism and the same kinds of problems that have existed in the juvenile delinquency system up to the present. That seems to me to be a serious mistake.
Another instance, which has not been touched on at any length, is that the law, in giving certain rights to young people, is not in fact doing it well enough. For example, take the problem of the use of evidence. Clause 56 of the bill provides that the law relating to the admissibility of statements made by persons accused of committing offences applies in respect of young persons. Then it goes through the instances where no oral or written statement given by a young person is admissible unless the statement is voluntary; unless the person who took the statement explained in language appropriate to his age and understanding that the young person has no obligation to make a statement and that any statement may be used against him; and that a young person has the right to counsel. As well, that the young person, even before the statement is made, must be given a reasonable opportunity to consult with counsel and so on. Those things are all enumerated.
It is also said that, generally speaking, before a young person makes a statement he or she will be informed of all their rights, that they will be read out and the young person will be able to see his or her counsel before a statement is made, and unless the statement complies with these requirements it will not be admissible in the youth court. Then again, as always, the government is concerned more with administrative convenience than with the hard notion that we must take rights seriously, that if we take rights seriously they are going to be inconvenient to the state. Clause 56(3) states:
The requirements set out in paragraphs (2)(b), (c) and (d) do not apply in respect of oral statements where they are volunteered by the young person to a peace officer or other person in authority before that person has had a reasonable opportunity to comply with those requirements.
If that paragraph is not big enough to drive a truck through, then I do not know what is. All the statements made by young people will be oral statements. All the statements, according to the police officers, will be made voluntarily. The onus clearly will be on the young person to show that the statement was not made voluntarily; that he was not told he had the right to counsel; that he was not instructed about all of those things. At age 14, a child is not going to ask to make a written statement. A child will say all sorts of things out of fear in response to the peculiar atmosphere of a police station. I think

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
it is very odd indeed that, on the one hand, the government is pretending it is giving rights to young people, that it is providing them with the kind of protection which should be part and parcel of our legal system, while on the other hand it is doing the kind of thing which we have come to expect of the government, namely, that where obviously there must be exceptions, we let an exception be made for oral statements. As I said before, oral statements will now be the practice, as they have been in the past, as far as young people are concerned. We have really provided no protection to our young people when we pretend that is what we have done.
1 mentioned that there were other problems in association with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, problems associated with the definition of what it means to be a young offender, and problems, if you like, at the age periphery where the juvenile delinquency system blends into the criminal justice system. In my view, we have offered very little guidance to our juvenile courts, our youth courts and the judges who preside over those courts as to under what circumstances we think cases should be transferred. We have provided very little protection to young people from being transferred into the criminal justice system. Not enough has been done in that regard. 1 would have thought this was one of the clear, rough-edged, difficult problems that we have. 1 admit there is no easy answer, but we have not provided anything like sufficient guidance to those people who are being asked to exercise such important discretion over the liberty of a subject of the Crown, which is really what our juvenile judges are being asked to decide.
The hon. member for Burnaby has emphasized the importance of a specified age. The hon. member for Durham-North-umberland has indicated he supports the concept of an age. 1 heard the Solicitor General's (Mr. Kaplan) speech on this bill. 1 cannot understand his reasoning or how he can talk so happily and so casually about allowing provinces to opt in or opt out with respect to certain age groups when this is the fundamental feature of the charter of rights. The notion of rights in Canada is that there are certain fundamental rights from which no province can opt out. You cannot have a country where people are being treated dramatically differently in one part of the country from another. You cannot have one criminal justice system where people in one province are treated so differently from people in another. Being treated as a youthful offender and being tried, convicted and sentenced under the criminal justice system is very different indeed. If the federal government does not have a clear notion of what the juvenile age is and what the rationale is, then 1 cannot understand it.
My basic preference, and this was set out by my colleague for Burnaby, would be for the youth court to have exclusive jurisdiction over dealing with all offenders up to the age of 18. The age of majority is 18. I agree with the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland that all ages such as the age of majority are arbitrary. Some of us can get very old indeed and not achieve a great deal of maturity. Other people are very mature at a young age. There has to be a standard set by Parliament. I suggest the logic clearly is that if the age of
majority is 18, then we categorize people under the age of 18 as not being subject to the rigours and toughness of the Criminal Code.
Those are the essential points I wanted to make. There are some anomalies in this legislation. To put it mildly, it is regrettable that the government has chosen to introduce a new measure for our young people who, because of poverty in Canada, the decline in our sense of community, the collapse of community values and the difficulties so many young people have in finding employment, are increasingly coming into conflict with the law. It is most regrettable that the primary objective of this bill is not rehabilitation but to make children responsible for everything they do. Having said that, the government should have gone out of its way to protect the rights of young people in all circumstances. They have not done that.
The government should have done more to overcome the difficulties we have lived with for over 70 years with respect to the Juvenile Delinquents Act. It appears we are fated to continue to live with it because the government has not seen fit to deal with some of the most difficult issues. It did not say in the definition of a young offender under the age in that jurisdiction that the jurisdiction of the youth court is complete, final and absolute and it will not allow the anomalous situation of some young people being treated as criminals in some parts of Canada and others being treated differently.
I want to make one final comment. I can think of no issue that is of more importance to the people of my constituency than the question of how efficiently, fairly and well our criminal and juvenile justice systems work. Part of the frustration of everyday living is seeing one's children come into conflict with the law for any of the reasons I have mentioned. The frustration that is created is endemic to the federal system, as pointed out by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland. This is because the federal government is responsible for the setting of the rules and the provincial governments are responsible for administering them and for funding. Frustrations are created if we have a turnstile type of justice, a revolving door in the juvenile courts.
We can understand the problems, frustration and ill-feeling toward the whole of the criminal justice system that is created. If a person's house is broken into time and time again and that person can see no end to the process, clearly the respect that person feels for the criminal justice system is limited. It leads to authoritarian responses to many other problems. On the other hand, if we have a system which deals with youth unfairly, arbitrarily or too harshly, we get into the situation where young people have no respect, not simply for the law, but for the community values which our law is said to represent.
I cannot resist saying that if we had a greater sense of community in Canada, that if we did not regard our communities simply as a place to make money off each other but as places where we treat each other with compassion and dignity, the rate of crime would decrease. Our sense of alienation from
May 12, 1981

one another would decrease. The kind of injustices that meet young people would also decrease.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on the second reading of Bill C-61, the Young Offenders Act, the repeal of the 73-year-old Juvenile Delinquents Act, and in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), on which you are yet to rule, which would in the interests of equal justice to all Canadians make one age, whether 16, 17 or 18, applied uniformly across Canada, whether in Nanaimo or St. John's, Newfoundland.
Before getting into my main remarks, may I, as did my colleague for Durham-Northumberland, express my concern about the fact that the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) did not even bother to join us this afternoon, nor indeed has his parliamentary secretary. Looking at the government benches, I see no cabinet minister present this afternoon for discussion of a very important bill. Perhaps I might be permitted to quote the Solicitor General who, on April 15, was lecturing the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland for being unavoidably absent from the chamber. I quote:
-the top priority of the members of Parliament should be to attend to the requirements of this chamber.
That is what he said, with servitude. I must confess that my annoyance is doubtless aggravated by the fact that the Solicitor General last month led my office to believe that this bill would not be discussed on April 15 in the absence of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland and myself. In fact, the bill was called on that day when both of us were absent from the chamber. Five members of my party spoke on second reading on April 15 and today. I will try to avoid repeating what they have said.
First, however, let me agree strongly that the outgoing Juvenile Delinquents Act is anachronistic today for many reasons. For one thing, it is a basic precept of our justice system that proscribed conduct must be clearly stated; but your child or mine, Mr. Speaker, could be found delinquent under the Juvenile Delinquents Act omnibus section for the vaguest type of conduct, such as sexual immorality or even for being uncontrollable, incorrigible or unmanageable. In short, status offences for juveniles and conviction by courts on a whole range of undefined acts were commonplace.
For another, the Juvenile Delinquents Act is replete with legislative foolishness. For example, one provision, which authorizes the waiver of serious charges such as murder against a juvenile, requires, among other things, that it must be first established to the satisfaction of a juvenile court judge that transfer is in the best interests of the juvenile, since in an adult court he or she will face adult sanctions. It has long seemed to me that it can logically never be in the best interests of a child-I am not talking here about the interests of society-to be transferred. The legal contortions necessary for a judge to waive must be enormous in view of the way that important provision in the Juvenile Delinquents Act is worded.
Young Offenders Act
Where is Canadian society just now in terms of crime committed by juveniles? Only last week, in talking with about 30 high school students in an inner city high school in Edmonton, the following points, among others, emerged, and this astounds me. The school I am speaking about, like five others in the city of Edmonton, has a full-time policeman every school day during the year, and has had since last year. Last year in a corridor a teacher was stabbed in the knee. I am told that recently there has been a problem with drugs, including hard drugs, and even some juvenile prostitution in that school. Two students told me of separate incidents in which different children under ten years of age had stolen items from neighbourhood homes. These occurrences took place at one school in one western Canadian city, not in New York or Detroit.
What is happening elsewhere across Canada? I do not quote very often from members of that other place, especially Liberal members, but Senator Florence Bird was quoted in a current issue of Maclean's magazine on this subject. She was speaking of violent crime statistics in Canada and is reported as follows:
What is particularly scary (about violent crime statistics in Canada) is the 60 per cent increase in violent juvenile delinquency from 1974 to 1978. Most shocking of all is the increase of violence by the young against themselves. In the past decade the suicide rate increased 59 per cent for young people aged 15 to 19.
Even more alarming, in my view, is the situation in respect of young people south of the border. I think it is clear that what is happening in the United States has had a bearing on much of what is contained in this bill. What is currently happening there frequently is an indication of what will be happening in Canada in five or ten years.
Let me read a few quotations from a book entitled "Criminal Violence, Criminal Justice" by Charles Silberman, published in 1978. Silberman is a layman who spent six years examining the crime epidemic in his country, and he has produced, in my opinion, an extraordinarily perceptive work, as perhaps only a layman could do. For example, he states at page 34:
-the youth culture emerged (in 1960s) as a major socializing force, taking over a large part of the burden traditionally carried by parents, teachers, clergymen and other adults.
Still on page 34 he states:
Initiation into heroin use is a phenomenon of youth: Two users in three begin using the drug between the ages of 15 and 21, with the great concentration occurring at age 18-
At page 35 he states:
-a teenager's status often depends on the ability to buy the "right" records and wear the "right" clothes. The adolescent need for money, combined with the weakening of adult social controls, has provided a lethal crimogenic force.
At page 311 he states:
The problem is not that juvenile courts are too lenient, but that they are too lenient toward the wrong people-
Mr. Silberman in his chapter on juvenile justice quotes from Judge William White, a juvenile court judge in Chicago speaking on this subject, as follows:

May 12, 1981

But looking at the (juvenile justice) record I am reminded of the Peanuts cartoon showing him sadly leaving the ball field with the scoreboard showing "Visitors 99, Home Team 0", "Ugh", he says, "How could it happen when we were so sincere."
Let me quote again from page 354 as follows:
In most states, juvenile court jurisdiction ends at age 18, since 16 and 17-year olds account for more than half of all juvenile arrests for violent crimes and 45 per cent of burglary arrests, that two-year difference in the age of jurisdiction, (between New York State with 16 and states having 18 as the age of majority) has an extraordinary impact on the number of cases that come before a juvenile court and on the way these cases are handled-
Finally, let me come to the more specific aspects of this bill and mention some of my major concerns. First, I would speak on the ages contemplated in Bill C-61. The minimum age for the youth offenders act criminal responsibility is to be 12 years rather than seven as in the old Juvenile Delinquents Act, as I think other speakers have mentioned. Obviously the provinces are expected to enact their own legislation to deal with barred conduct by children between the ages of seven and 12, and to pay all related costs. I was told just a few minutes ago, and I am afraid I must agree, that today there are in fact some children between the ages of seven to 12 who do commit serious crimes. Can all the provinces with their different financial situations be expected to absorb these related costs? Will there be a judicial checkerboard, to use that now familiar phrase, caused by this federal initiative?
The maximum age for liability under the youth offenders act is to be 18 years, subject to reduction at the request of an individual province to 16 or 17. As you know, Mr. Speaker, our government proposed a uniform maximum age of 16 years, subject to accepting a higher age of 17 or 18 only if all provinces agreed. The hon. member for Durham-Northumber-land mentioned this. This is why there is now an amendment before the House, and I am pleased to speak in support of it if you rule it to be in order.
This concept will be a major source of federal-provincial controversy. Obviously that is the case. Alberta and Ontario, which use the age of 16 as a cut-off, obviously want this to remain, in part because of the large cost of the administrative implications, particularly if the juvenile net is widened to include 17 and 18-year-olds. This could result in more of their youth residents going to youth detention centres, those who are now subject to adult sanctions and corrections.
1 wish someone opposite could tell me, through you, Mr. Speaker, whether the federal government is being conciliatory to the provinces only because it wishes to avoid increased costs. Why otherwise is the government now tolerating a checkerboard Canada in the justice field? Different standards of programs in different provinces for youth are certainly going to remain as a result of this measure, and obviously poorer provinces will continue to have inferior programs because of their tax bases.
1 am told that evidently the Solicitor General does not want one age, as we propose, because this would cause a confrontation with the provinces. In view of what the federal government has done recently in terms of confronting the provinces in matters involving, in some cases, their exclusive jurisdiction, I
can only say that this is a laugh. 1 would remind him that his duties or responsibilities under the existing Constitution include criminal law, so nobody can complain that he is invading provincial spheres here by having one age, such as we can and do when he invades areas of exclusive provincial responsibility under the constitutional proposals.
The point mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) was that Section 15 of the charter of rights, if found legal by the Supreme Court, would ban discrimination on the basis of age, among other things. It seems self-evident that any differences in age under this bill would be struck down by the courts. Because of the particular wording chosen in Section 15, I seriously wonder as well if any age chosen would not similarly be struck down as being unconstitutional discrimination against young people on the basis of age. I have a strong feeling that no one on the other side has thought about this point.
In respect of the matter of youth records, this bill requires the destruction of these records after a crime-free qualifying period, presumably on the basis that many young persons would not in practice apply for the same without the automatic feature. In fairness, I must say that in our proposal in 1979 the records would have been sealed, with limited access for research purposes.
Another point is that the right of youths to counsel at all stages of proceedings is proposed in the bill, and I favour that strongly; but will the courts interpret this to mean the right to duty counsel alone or to more? Once again, the various legal aid plans in this area will presumably differ, as now, substantially across the country. Are we giving equal justice to all young people in that sense?
The important matter of diversion is left essentially to provincial choice. Would it not be wiser to lay out some clearer criteria or standard so that the concept carries, hopefully, the same substance throughout the country? Why should diversion be allowed in one province and not in the next, if what we are dealing with here is a matter of exclusive federal responsibility for the criminal law?
At present under the Juvenile Delinquents Act violations of provincial and municipal statutes constitute Juvenile Delinquents Act offences. No more, of course, under this bill. Only breaches of the Criminal Code and other federal statutes and regulations will be the bases for conviction under this legislation. Should there not, therefore, be at least some phasing-in time available for the provinces wishing to enact complementary legislation? It seems to me self-evident that there should be a phasing-in period for such provinces.
I come now to what I consider to be the most controversial part of the bill, and I stress that I am speaking for myself alone on this and not for my party. I have a feeling that a large number of Canadians would share my concerns about the feature in the bill which would completely revoke the concept of vicarious liability of parents or guardians which existed under Section 22 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act in favour of
May 12, 1981

making only youths themselves responsible-including financially-for their acts.
Up until now, if a group of rampaging young people-I will not give them a sex-broke into a school or community hall and reduced the windows or whatever to rubble, a juvenile court had the authority to impose damages on their parents where it found that the parents in effect had contributed to the offence "by neglecting to exercise due care of the child." It strikes me that assuming such a feature is, and was, constitutionally valid as being incidental to Parliament's criminal law power, a great many Canadians will want it to remain for suitable, special circumstances. In fairness, the proposal of my colleague, the solicitor general of the time, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, in 1979, would also have eliminated possible parental liability, but personally I am not at all persuaded that such a feature should not be added to this bill, presumably in committee. I see that at least one of my colleagues other than the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland supports that view.

Indeed, on the basis of my limited experience with juvenile crime I think it would be a serious mistake to remove it. I know that some will say that society could always proceed against parents under a "contributing to juvenile delinquency" section, which I gather is to be added to the Criminal Code in the future, but why not leave this string in the legislation's bow as well? I am not saying it has to be used often, but I think this should be available.
Someone said the other day that the cost-sharing aspects- as an economist, Mr. Speaker, you would appreciate this-of the bill are likely to consume at least two weeks of committee time alone on this bill. I agree. This is, of course, because the bill revokes-I think this is important-the transfer of jurisdiction over youths made by the Juvenile Delinquents Act to the provincial sphere, thereby making the provinces no longer eligible in law for the $65 million or so they now receive yearly for shared-cost juvenile services under the Canada Assistance Plan. It is true that clause 69 of the bill authorizes new financial arrangements with the provinces at the discretion of Ottawa, and there may be some naive folk on this side or the other-not that we have any naive folk on this side-who believe that the levels of financial support present since 1965 or 1968 will continue.
I note that a minister is present now. I ask those opposite who have responsibility what incentive rests with the Solicitor General to enter into any such agreements now if this bill is passed. Surely the government-or the minister-should be up front enough to state its intentions publicly in this regard, at least so that perhaps it might have something it could renounce later on.
There are other aspects of the bill which are worthy of comment-I will not take up the time of the House because I know there is a large number of people who want to speak- including its detention and bail features, transfer to adult court provisions, privacy of proceedings, disposition of cases,
Young Offenders Act
release from custody, review of dispositions, appeals, fingerprinting and photographs, but I believe I touched earlier on the major areas of appropriate public concern. Hopefully this debate will serve to have interested Canadians everywhere, including members of Parliament, take a careful look at this very important measure.
In closing, I might say that if any member of the public hearing or seeing me wishes to appear at the committee hearings, I would be grateful if he or she would let any of my party colleagues or myself know as quickly as possible.
