Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer I am interested professionally in this piece of legislation. As a parent-indeed, as a grandparent-I am personally affected by the legislation. It behooves us all as Canadians to be interested in legislation affecting the youth of our country. It is for that reason I am particularly pleased to be able to join in the debate on this bill dealing with the proposed Young Offenders Act.
While I am in large part in support of the bill, I cannot accept the position of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) that we must rush through the debate at second reading. As the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) this afternoon shows, there is no legislation which cannot be improved, and this legislation is no exception.
Having said that, I note that this legislation has been long in coming. We have been reminded of that fact several times already. I should not belabour that particular point, but I would like to point out that the Juvenile Delinquents Act as we know it has been in effect for 52 years. We should pay some tribute to those who have been charged with the responsibility of administering that act.
I would be remiss if I did not join my colleagues in this House in stating that we owe a debt to the juvenile justice community. It is a credit to the juvenile court process, juvenile court justices, law enforcement personnel, social workers and, indeed, the provinces that serious and widespread injustices to the youth of this country have not taken place. The potential for abuses and injustices has been there and present over that long period of time, and it is refreshing and encouraging in these troubled and divisive times to see that that justice community has performed and is performing in an exemplary manner.
Although we in the Progressive Conservative party are not examining this bill in a partisan manner, it would be unfair if we did not mention the fact that, in relation to the proposed Young Offenders Act, we in this House owe to the predecessor of the Solicitor General, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, some credit for the legislation now being introduced. The Clark government made the Young Offenders Act a priority order of the day, and I cannot help but feel that in so doing it gave much impetus to the Solicitor General to bring forward the legislation now before us.

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
I must also add that I am disappointed that the minister responsible for the administration of this act is not present in this House as we debate his bill.
Legislation concerning a large segment of our population, or as large a part of it as this group represents, permits endless tangential discussions that can cause us not only to lose sight of the issue, but to cloud the issue to the extent that the good is lost with the bad. Consequently, I wish to discuss some of the measures specifically and make some general comments with respect to the process.
The Young Offenders Act has much to recommend it, particularly in the strengthening of the alleged offender's rights and the formalizing of a diversion procedure. It is hard to believe that in 1981 we are only just coming into the right of appeal, the right of legal representation, and the right to a sentence review for our young people. It is also surprising that our judges have had to govern their courts without the benefit of formal procedures and the benefit of meaningful sentencing options. Recognizing this fact, and recognizing that in this matter of sentencing options diversion is long overdue for formal sanctioning, I am at a loss to understand why the proposed act is as vague as it is.
Under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, an alleged offender would, so to speak, have his or her day in court. But in many of those instances, that day in court was not necessary, nor was it even desirable, and the judge had to take it upon himself to assume that responsibility of indicating an alternate course of action. Now, under the proposed legislation, alleged offenders would be given the opportunity, if one wants to be optimistic for the moment, to bypass the court by accepting a prescribed punishment. This implies, naturally enough, that guilt is not in question and that the crime is not a serious one. Bill C-61 does not set out definite or specific guidelines to follow for diversion. Hence, a youngster could be coerced into accepting an alternative measure rather than appearing in court, and perhaps, if he had appeared in court, being found not guilty. I recognize the words in Bill C-61, and I trust the committee will take another look at Section 3 of the act.
The number of sentencing options have a similarly vague application. Under Section 20, subsection (1), the judge would be given ten definite sentencing options, or if there was no conflicting combination of each, an added eleventh permitting the court to "impose on the young person such other reasonable and ancillary conditions as it deems advisable and in the best interest of the young person and the public". Now, that is faith, indeed! Further, despite the wide range of sentencing options available, there are no provisions in the act indicating, let alone stating, which offences should receive which degree of sentencing. This quandary may well return us to the current state of affairs, as indicated by one of the earlier speakers, as well as that facing judges in days gone by under the previous Juvenile Delinquents Act.
These two areas, sentencing and diversion, are essentially good ones simply in need of sharper definition. The same
cannot be said for the lack of a uniform maximum age. I want to address this issue as others have done before me.
We have recently concluded, for the moment, a very lengthy and, yes, tiring debate on the Constitution. We heard repeatedly from the government benches that any checkerboard concept was an abomination, something to regard as anathema. Now we are being told by the Solicitor General that there is consensus today that uniformity of standards and law should be extended throughout the country. But what do we find in this proposed legislation? An accommodation of individual provinces which have expressed different positions with respect to the maximum age.
The Solicitor General goes on in his March 14 speech to state that this position reflects the different services and resources of the various provinces for dealing with young offenders. On April 15 he added that it also reflected differing philosophies with respect to the age of maturity. Mr. Speaker, this concern of differing attitudes, resources and services leaves me not just a little concerned and confused. Surely, as Canadians, there should be a uniform application of the Criminal Code right across this land of ours, and just as surely young Canadians wherever they live should be entitled to the same benefits and be subject to the same restrictions and responsibilities that this act provides.
The confusion is augmented when one considers the raising of the minimum age for criminal responsibility from seven to 12 years. I support this change. All of us do. Most if not all the previous speakers have supported it, as have eight of the ten provinces. Two provinces did not support this change, yet the Solicitor General did not allow this to prevent him from introducing a uniform minimum age. Why, may I ask, was there not the same insistence that there be a uniform maximum age?
I do not enter into any partisan approach. My concern with the lack of uniformity on the maximum age does not lie with my constitutional quarrel with this government, but with the rights of our young people. The charter of rights, Section 15, prohibits discrimination on the basis of age. How could the Young Offenders Act fail to violate that section, that clause, this right, when a 17-year-old could be treated differently in one province as opposed to another?
If nothing can be done to implement uniformity, then I think that the committee should consider alternate means of ensuring a youth's equality before the law. Perhaps an "overage" youth in one province could be permitted to apply to a court in another province that treats the youths of his age. I recognize the problems of bureaucracy, the expense; but I urge careful examination of that uniformity clause or alternates to meet the need of equal application of the law in any province of this country.
Of supreme importance is close and meaningful liaison with the provincial authorities. This act will increase the burden of the various child welfare acts of the provinces by adding to them a whole new category of children, those between seven and 12 years of age. As well, the proposed legislation has dropped all provincial and municipal laws, bylaws, and ordi-
May 12, 1981

nances from their domain, leaving them within the provincial authorities. Without liaison work, we shall create a judicial morass that could take years to untangle. I trust the committee will be cognizant of that fact when it enters its consideration of these clauses.
Those are primary concerns with the proposed legislation. There are other points of lesser importance, but they are worth mentioning at this stage. The maximum fine of $1,000, for example, strikes me as being high. Remember we are talking of persons under the age of 18. We do not want to encourage another crime to pay off a previous one. The review procedure is potentially bureaucratic in nature. It is a bureaucratic monster with automatic reviews, optional reviews, progress reports and supplementary progress report material. The juvenile courts had to deal with almost 91,000 cases in 1978. Multiply whatever percentage of that number you like as qualifying for a review, or for a review of a review, and you have created tons of paperwork and an abundance of bureaucratic work.
Finally, I think the destruction of the criminal record after a qualifying period of good behaviour is a welcome change. But, as a legal community colleague of mine pointed out to me, employment application forms are slowly switching to the question: "Have you ever been charged with a criminal offence?" This problem would perhaps be best addressed by amendments to the human rights legislation both at the federal and provincial levels. These criticisms and recommendations are all matters that I would like to see the committee discuss seriously.
The proposed Young Offenders Act, as I said earlier, has far more in it to recommend than to criticize. It provides the three basic elements that the Progressive Conservative party believes to be imperative: young offenders have been charged with a greater responsibility for their actions, they have been given stronger rights under the law, and there is greater flexibility in, and therefore greater hope for, rehabilitation options. We also welcome the end of the so-called status offences-the omnibus charge of delinquency. These "offences" smeared our youth with a broad brush and have rendered the words "juvenile delinquent" odious in connotation. Our young people have difficulty enough without having labels applied to them that live long past the age of majority.
I would like to commend the Solicitor General for the submission of this legislation. Subject to the comments I have made today, I support the legislation. I am sure the committee will examine the reservations I have put forward with serious intent. Let us hope that we can better this legislation in the future as it affects our community, not only for today but for tomorrow. Having waited 52 years for change is far too long.
Young Offenders Act

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my participation in this debate will be confined to one or two aspects of the bill and, principally, to omissions in the bill. I do not know whether these omissions were deliberate or an oversight, but I propose to deal with them when the time comes.
The previous intervener mentioned the odium connected with the title "juvenile delinquent". We welcome the change of that title to "young offender". I think it is a step in the right direction in ensuring that those misguided young people who do have confrontations with the law will not carry with them for all time the obloquy of being designated a delinquent. It has a pejorative meaning. "Young offender" is a better designation.
Under the Juvenile Delinquents Act there were very important provisions, some of which have already been mentioned, with respect to parental involvement in making restitution. 1 think the principle of restitution is a valid one. Perhaps when we get to committee it will be possible to make amendments to the provisions of the Young Offenders Act to ensure that there is adequate parental responsibility assigned.
My principal concern is with the failure to make any reference whatsoever in the Young Offenders Act to provisions which were made in Section 20 of the Juvenille Delinquents Act. That section deals with the options open to the court to deal in a fatherly, parental or guiding fashion, if you like, with

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
delinquents who may have been involved, for good reason or bad, or as a result of peer pressure, in activities which brought them before the court. Under the present act the courts are able to deal with the youthful offender either by diverting them to probation officers or by ensuring that they return to their parents, fosters homes or other institutions which will keep them out of the court system. The court can take this action under the existing legislation without having the youthful offender carry with him for all time the stigma of being labelled a delinquent for having had a confrontation with the law, for having gone through what must be a very unsettling process. The process sometimes brings out the very worst in the youth. It causes him to overreact and before you know it he is back in the hands of the law again.
The provisions of the young offenders bill provide for three different groups of individuals who may be dealt with in one form or another. Presumably, there are those who up to the age of 12 will be dealt with under provincial law. I say "presumably" because it is not clear in my mind that there is a consistent method of dealing with youthful offenders right across the country-those under the age of 12. Someone mentioned an offence which could be committed by someone at one end of a bridge spanning the Ottawa River, and another person committing the same kind of offence at the other end of that bridge would be dealt with in a totally different manner. This could occur in other jurisdictions where there are provincial boundaries involved.
There are financial implications of the administration of that law which would be solely and wholly borne by the provinces for offences committed by those under the age of 12. Has that been made absolutely clear to the provincial attorneys general? We are not sure of that and I think we will want to clear that matter up in the committee. We will want to be sure that representatives of the attorneys general departments across the country have an opportunity to go before the committee, to make their cases in law and to make their cases in financial terms as well. That is absolutely essential. At the same time, it may very well be possible to harmonize, if not make common law, across this land for offenders under the age of 12.
It is not generally recognized, and I suppose it is not all that easy to state, that if one looks at crime, disregarding for the moment motor vehicle incidents or confrontations with the law, from 50 per cent to 60 per cent of crime is committed by juveniles. We do not like to face this fact, because our police are expected to be the great sturdy men that they are. I know from experience in my own community that they are community workers. More power to them for that. They are not to be denigrated on that account but should be praised. They deserve all our praise for responding to that community effort in dealing with young offenders.
In one particular municipality in my riding, about 70 per cent to 80 per cent of incidents of breaking the law, disregarding motor vehicle incidents, are committed by persons considered to be juveniles. In another area where 6,800 offences were reported with only 1,100 apprehensions, 55 per cent of those apprehensions were of juveniles. Those were followed by convictions, so that means that out of the 6,800 offences committed, only 500 of the 1,100 apprehensions involved crimes known to have been committed by juveniles. By extrapolating, one could say that of the 6,800, perhaps 3,600 or even 4,000 of the offences committed and reported were committed by juveniles.
Those who are administering the law are concerned on two scores. They are concerned by the absence in the young offenders bill of some means of dealing with them other than through the courts; of not having them committed firmly to a confrontation with the law. There must be some way of dealing with those offenders between the ages of 12 and 17 other than through confrontation with a judge in the solemn dignity of a court procedure. That absence could be rectified in the young offenders bill.
Once this has been discussed with the administrators of the law in the provinces and they agree that this particular lacuna should be closed, that there should be a provision in the new legislation to deal in a more gentle way with those offenders who can be shown to have become involved in their confrontation with the law for reasons that were not long-term criminal but were, rather, usually in response to a challenge, I hope there will be an opportunity to rectify matters. What child will not respond to a challenge, to a dare? These "crimes"-and I put the word in quotation marks-can be eliminated from the system and dealt with under the provisions of Section 20 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, but there is no method that I can see in the Young Offenders Act to deal with them in a softer manner.
I agree entirely with the hon. member for Durham-North-umberland (Mr. Lawrence) that one of the great failures in the bill before us is its refusal to face the need for an upper limit on that second category of miscreants or offenders above the age of 12 and up to the age of 16, 17 or 18. We must fix that age. That is the second group of individuals dealt with in a special way. Beyond that age they are assumed to be of the age of responsibility and will face the consequences of their acts under the criminal law if they have committed a crime, or under other aspects of our law.
To go back to the statistics that I cited a few minutes ago about the preponderance of crime committed by those who are under age, whatever that means, a good number of these are in the age bracket of ten, 11 and approaching 12. That is a dreadful thing to have to admit. I do not derive any satisfaction whatsoever from stating that young criminal elements are being developed at that age, but it is the case; there is no question about it. I have this on the most firm authority of those who deal with young offenders on a day to day basis and who can see the formation of the chronic criminal prior to the 12-year-old limit set in the new bill. I wonder whether 12 is the correct age to insert in this bill.
May 12, 1981

I have said, of course, that the provincial legislations across the country will be dealing with the pre-12-year-old, but since there is no assurance that this aspect will be dealt with in a consistent fashion from one coast to the other, perhaps there is a case to be made, which can be made in committee. We could reduce the requirement of age 12 to, say, that of age ten if the experience of other administrators of the law, parole officers and those who are dealing with the corrective aspects of youthful misbehaviour, can prove that it is a critical age and that it is an age group that might better be dealt with under the provisions of the Young Offenders Act. I would like to see not only representatives of the Attorney General before the committee, but also those who have been dealing with the young offenders in family court and in the parole system and so hear their experience directly. This may enable us to make the necessary amendments to make the act not only a better one but one which will be uniform in application across the country.
One of the criticisms levelled at the act is the media treatment which has been given to it. Not long ago there was a suggestion, whether in a headline or in the text of an article, that the new laws coming into effect for juvenile offenders would be tougher; in other words, more severe. This, of course, raised the expectations of those members of the community who felt the law is not tough enough because there is altogether too much vandalism and vandals are able to get away with their misdeeds. Raising the expectations of the general public in this way is a media abuse. 1 do not know whether it was deliberately done on the part of the government to indicate that it is really out to crack down on juvenile delinquents, or whether it was just the manner in which the statements, publications or documents issued by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) were considered by the press.
An ancillary comment made through stories in the media was that juveniles would now have the right to appeal. In my province this right exists today. There is no need to suggest that some new provisions will come into effect when those provisions already exist. The right to appeal is certainly one of them. There are provisions in my province also for retaining a lawyer to assist youthful offenders under the legal aid system. This bill before us now provides that youthful offenders will have lawyers. That is not new, nor should it be broadcast as new. Perhaps I am speaking solely about my province. Perhaps the right to legal counsel does not exist in other provinces. But this particular provision, provided that we get the age spread correct under which the offender does have the right to legal counsel, is not all that new, and it is a mistake to characterize it as though it were.
There is a definition in the Juvenile Delinquents Act which defines a child. A child is any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of 16 years or such other age as may be directed in any province pursuant to subsection (2). The definition of a child in the bill before us means a person who is, or, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, appears to be under the age of 12. The definition of a child is a person under
Young Offenders Act
the age of 16 in the existing law and under the age of 12 in the proposed bill.
Another criticism brought to my attention is that no provision is made within this bill to ascertain the age which determines whether the offender falls within provincial jurisdiction as being under the age when he would fall under this particular bill, or whether he should fall under this bill. There is no provision either for the parent or the guardian to be notified that his child or his ward has been charged with an offence.
In this respect I suppose this bill is intruding into the affairs of the family in a manner which I think is quite unacceptable. When any member of a family under that legal age-yet to be determined either 16'/2, 17 or 18-is charged with an offence, surely it is right and proper that the parent or guardian of that young person should be notified of the offence charged. 1 think it only right and proper also that the parent or guardian should be required to appear in the court to attest to the age of the child by whatever means he has at his disposal. The offender may be 11 years and ten months. This bill refers to a person who is, or, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, appears to be under the age of 12 years. How is evidence of age obtained? There is no requirement that evidence be obtained. There is provision within the existing bill to obtain that evidence. The parent or guardian is required to show that the offender is of the age required to be dealt with under this particular measure. I think that matter ought to be corrected as well.
One final matter worries me somewhat. It is related to the earlier ones and I draw the attention of the House to it. In my opinion, it will be worth examining in greater detail in committee. Specifically, I am speaking of clauses 71, 72 and 73 of the bill which deal with amendments to the Criminal Code. Sections 12 and 13 to the Criminal Code are repealed and Section 12 is replaced by a provision which introduces the 12-year age limit again. Clause 71 removes a provision from the Criminal Code which deserves to remain in some way or other. I would like to read Section 13 of the Criminal Code because of the loss of that particular provision as a result of clause 71.1 read Section 13 of the Criminal Code:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was seven years of age or more-
That, of course, is going up to 12.
-but under the age of fourteen years, unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong.
It is that final section to which I allude and which has a role to play in any matter where offences are committed against society or against another person. I quote it again so that we will be reminded of it:
-unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong.
Are we going to eliminate that notion of rightness and wrongness from our law, the element of moral responsibility which we should be inculcating in our young people? The
9508

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
young person will say that because it is not there, there is no need to worry whether it is right or wrong, the judge will decide.
This is a matter of moral responsibility. Like many other things in our society in the past ten or 12 years, the transformation is being brought about in the moral attitudes of people toward one another and to their society by changes such as this. I deplore the loss of that phrase. I feel it must be restored somewhere within the law. Not only I but social workers with whom ! have spoken about this matter are prepared to attest that youthful offenders are competent to know that some of the offences they commit are wrong. They should not be discouraged from judging in their own mind the rightness, wrongness and consequences of what they are planning, are in the course of, or have performed.
Those are the comments I wish to make at this stage. I hope that when the bill goes before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, as those who have spoken before me have mentioned, there will be an opportunity to have brought before us representatives from the attorneys general of the provinces and possibly from the provincial finance departments so that they will be able to judge the fiscal implications of the bill. 1 implore those who will be sitting on this committee to make arrangements so that the administrators of the law, those in a position of responsibility and guidance, such as parole officers and those who have concern for these young people, who see where they are going wrong and how they can be helped, will have an opportunity to appear before the committee and make their case and help improve this bill.

speechtext:
An amendment was proposed earlier by the hon. member for Durham-Northumb-erland, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona. The Chair wishes to advise hon. members that the amendment is found to be in order. Consequently I will read it and then debate can proceed. Mr. Lawrence, seconded by Mr. Kilgour, moves:
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"-this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-61, an act respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, because the bill rejects the fundamental principle of equal treatment of all persons before the law by specifying that the act will apply to different age groups in different provinces."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to hear you rule that the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) is in order. I know there is general support for this legislation. At the same time I recognize that there are some inherent problems in the provisions and sometimes the language of the bill. Therefore, it would be good if members of the House would support this amendment in order that it might be drafted in a better form and have more acceptable support from hon. members.
Members who have been here for at least the past five years will know that I have had a continuing interest in legislation dealing with the welfare of children and young people, as well
as legislation that would protect the sanctity of the home. Therefore, 1 welcome this legislation, which has some aspects of reality in it. I hope it will provide some measures to deal with some of the problems we face in our society and some of the problems our young people face.
I begin by reiterating what some others have pointed out. There is a shift of emphasis in the title. Rather than speak about juvenile delinquents, we will now speak of young offenders. I see both an up side and a down side to that. There was a time when a young person involved in criminal activity was called a criminal. That is what he was, even though he was young. Society determined that because of the person's youth, it was not wholesome for someone 12, 14 or 16 years of age to be labelled a criminal, so a softer definition was given to his activity. He became a juvenile delinquent. After years of having this term heaped on young people, it is now a term of opprobrium and is no longer acceptable. It is a term of disgrace. We will now redefine what originally was a criminal and call him a young offender rather than a juvenile delinquent. I would point out that the behaviour has not necessarily changed. It is the definition of that behaviour which has changed. We really have not addressed the problem that that young person is facing.
While I welcome the change in title, I see an up side and a down side. Simply changing the definition will not solve the problem. It will not make that young person feel better about himself. That young person will feel rotten inside not because of the term "juvenile delinquent" or "young offender" which is attached to him, but because he has done something wrong. The best favour we can extend to that young person is to help him face the reality that he has done something wrong, not to soften the definition of what he has done or of what kind of person he is.
Maybe some kind of reality therapy is what we ought to prescribe because he is in fact a young criminal. To call that person a young offender may, ironically in terms of the government's legislation, go some distance to meet that need because it is no longer advantageous to call him a delinquent. The term "delinquent" is a pretty soft term. That is why it was written that way. The person is actually an offender if he has offended the law and offended society. Calling such a person a young offender is actually a little closer to reality than calling him a juvenile delinquent. I see some value in redefining the term and calling the legislation young offenders legislation rather than the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
That leads me to a second point by way of introduction. In far too many instances we have tried to soften our criminal statistics by changing the definition of a crime. When I was young, if a young person was caught shoplifting he was stealing, but today he is shoplifting. You cannot change the nature of the offence by redefining it. You may improve the statistics but you do not change the nature of the offence. It seems to me that far too often we are trying to make society
May 12, 1981

look better by redefining the crime instead of dealing with the problem. 1 am concerned about that fact.
Let me speak about two particular aspects of this legislation which, I feel, are wanting, and both of which have been touched upon by previous speakers. I simply want to emphasize my concern about a lapse in this legislation which fails to deal with important aspects in the lives of young people if we are to help them face reality. If we continue this lapse through this legislation we will do them a disservice.
One aspect is that area which relieves parents of responsibility for the activities of their children. I know that this legislation, by taking the responsibility from the parents, is shifting it to the broad shoulders of society in general. In some instances that implies it is not the parents but, rather, it is society which is responsible for the behaviour of young people. In some cases that may be true. There may be certain instances where society in general has created the circumstances which have led young people to take part in criminal activity. It seems to me this is an extension of the kind of social engineering under which we have been labouring for the past generation or so. The thinkers in our society have come to believe that by tinkering with the social structure and by shifting responsibility, we address the problems. That is far from the reality. I think it is also an extension of the kind of economic determinism which has been part of the thinking of our society during the past generation, that it is because of economics that people go into a life of crime. Again there may be instances where people have been encouraged because of economics to go into lives of crime. It is fallacious reasoning to conclude that economics make people turn to crime. By relieving parents of their responsibility, we are asking society in general to accept that responsibility.
Let me illustrate the shift that is taking place. I was born at the beginning of the depression. I am not saying I caused it, but somehow the chronology coincided. I grew up during those depression years which, as members know, were some of the most poverty-ridden years of this country. My parents were parents of a large family during those very deprived years. My father used to go from a small town in Saskatchewan where we lived at the time, put his bike on the Grey Goose bus in Saskatchewan and travel to the Fraser Valley in British Columbia in order to find summer employment where there were still jobs during the summer months. He would then come back in time for the harvest in Saskatchewan to get day labour and make enough to put us through the winter.
In that small prairie town of one thousand or two thousand people we had one constable. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) will know of the town of Rosthern, and he is old enough to remember those years. We had one constable for the entire town, a small city we might call it today. We also had a curfew law. I remember standing on the wrong side of the sidewalk at about two minutes after nine o'clock, after the curfew bell had rung, when the constable, walking by and seeing my parents in the yard, motioned me to come into the yard. The town had a jail in the city hall, but it was usually empty, and this was at the time of our greatest
Young Offenders Act
depression. If poverty creates crime, that should have been the time when crime was the greatest, at least according to the economic determinism theory. Usually the jail was empty.
Let me bring you up to date. A few years ago the municipal council of Surrey decided it would help society if there were curfew legislation in Surrey. About two years ago it passed a curfew law which ordered young people to be home at eleven o'clock at night, particularly on weekends. That policy lasted about three Saturdays. At eleven o'clock at night, the RCM Police would go to the local hangouts, McDonald's or wherever they happened to be, pick up the kids who were under age and take them to the police station. They were not being put in jail but just taken there while the police got in touch with their parents. At two o'clock in the morning they were still phoning the parents to come and get their children. Because they were usually unable to find the parents to look after their children, the municipal council was not able to carry out that curfew policy.
This is what has happened in our society in terms of parental responsibility. Is it the responsibility of our police forces to look after young people under 16 years of age after eleven o'clock at night? I thought that when parents were raising children it was their responsibility to look after those children, not the responsibility of society. Therefore, I regret that the government, through this legislation, will further relieve parents of their accountability for raising children.
I am concerned about this move because of another consequence. If the government at this point is relieving parents of their accountability, at what point down the road will it prohibit parents from exercising their authority over their children? The first stage is relieving parents of responsibility and the second is prohibiting them from exercising authority. This will result in state intervention in family responsibilities. We do not have to go far outside our country to find examples of the state assuming full responsibility for looking after families. That to me spells the deterioration of a society. The first and most important institution in the land is the home, and whenever the state intervenes in the conduct of the home and takes away the authority of the home, society goes down the skids.
The second contradiction in this kind of economic determinism which says that society is responsible, because of the social scales in our society, for creating a life of crime is the fact that much of today's crime is in the affluent areas of our society. If it is poverty which creates crime, why is so much crime committed by the affluent people of our society? Why are many of the young offenders of our society coming from the high schools in the affluent sections of our cities? Why is it? Why is the worst kind of crime-and, in terms of dollars, the highest proportion of crime-white collar crime?
There are some hard realities we as a country have to face if we want to address the nature of crime in our country. If we are going to address the problem, we will have to conclude sooner or later that crime exists because people decide to

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
engage in criminal activity. They try to take shortcuts which run roughshod over the rights of other people. Parents decide that they are going to be irresponsible parents; young people decide that they are going to take advantage of their parents' irresponsibility, and sooner or later we have to have a law which says that parents and young people, and nobody else, will be held accountable for their actions. Parents and young people both have to be held accountable for their behaviour. One psychologist said, "You may have inherited that problem but you are responsible; you cannot pass it off on your parents forever; you cannot blame them forever." Sooner or later we must decide what kind of people we want to be, and there is no sense in kidding ourselves; we cannot pretend that we are doing young people a favour by suggesting that somebody else is responsible for their behaviour.
I suggest that the government would do all of Canada a favour if, at the committee stage, it re-evaluated the position it has taken on this section of the bill, replaced the section dealing with parental accountability for the behaviour of young people and made parents socially, and many times financially, accountable for the behaviour of their children.
Second, I agree in part with what the hon. member for Broadview-Greenview (Mr. Rae) indicated earlier this afternoon. He said that young people need the opportunity to experience and display a sense of atonement. I agree with that. Young people should not be locked in and labelled for life because of their behaviour at one particular stage of their lives. Society in many cases does act prejudicially against young people because of indiscretions, because of earlier rebellions, and sometimes because of false values having been given to them. They have engaged in activity which has been criminal, but they do not deserve to be labelled for life as young offenders, criminals or whatever definition we want to use. There has to be an opportunity for atonement. Young people deserve the opportunity to be trusted because there is very slim chance of atonement in young people if they are not going to be trusted. It begins with trust.
However, I add to what the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood said by saying that atonement or a confession of atonement is totally irrelevant unless there is also restitution. That is how we know people are serious and genuine about their confession of atonement. The apology of a person who says he is sorry for what he has done is not accepted if he does not also restore the thing he has taken, whether it is money, reputation or whatever it is. It is easy for a young person to have engaged in a breaking and entering, a shoplifting or a theft of an automobile and then to say, "I am sorry", but that is not good enough, even if he means it, because part of the formula for atonement-it is integrally related to atonement- is restitution.
I want to use an adult illustration. About a year and a half ago, a gentleman was convicted of a crime in the province of Quebec. He happened to be the head of an organization known as the Apostles of Infinite Love, a pseudo-Roman Catholic institution. Hon. members have all heard of the Apostles of Infinite Love. This gentleman was convicted of the abduction
of some of the children who were in his institution, and he was sentenced. He served his sentence, and a week or two ago he was released on parole, apparently on good behaviour. The fact is that he has not returned the children he abducted. He still has them in his so-called monastery at St. Jovite. He has supposedly atoned for his crime, but he has not restored the children.
This ludicrous situation makes a mockery of all law and all sense of justice. This man has been convicted. He has served his sentence. Legally he has atoned, but he still has the children, and he cannot be tried again for that offence. The system has now rewarded him because he cannot be tried again for that offence. How are we to get those children back?
When we have glaring examples like that of atonement without restitution, we reinforce all across society the belief that in many cases crime pays. It pays as long as one rides out the system. Is there not something in our legal system which says one has not atoned for one's crime until one restores what one has taken? How many cases are there in which individuals have been convicted of armed robbery, taken their loot and hidden it, ridden out their sentence and come back and lived off their loot? The famous train robbery in England is a case in point. One of the perpetrators has become a hero in England because he has been able to make a mockery of the so-called justice system. Why should we entrench in the proposed Young Offenders Act a concept which says a person can be convicted of a crime and atone for that crime by going through the penal system but that that person does not have to restore what he has taken? That is wrong. It is bad law. We ought not to let this go through third reading-not let it go through committee stage, let alone third reading, until we incorporate in this legislation the concept that one cannot atone unless one restores, and no crime has been atoned until there has been restitution.
These are two concepts that I believe are wanting in this legislation. I think that we would do an injustice to our young people if we presented to them a system which allows them to avoid facing the reality of life by escaping the reality of their behaviour and shunting that accountability on to the state. We are doing a disservice to parents by allowing them to shunt the responsibility for their children to the state. We are not teaching our young people the reality of life if we say that they can atone without having to restore. I think that is the rock bottom concept that we have to incorporate in this legislation before we give it third and final reading.

speechtext:
I would like to speak briefly on the young offenders bill, and particularly under five headings. I think the basis of the young offenders bill should be enshrined with the words "The objective to build and not to destroy".
I find that young people today who get their fun out of destroying things have made up their minds that they want to live that type of a life; and it is essential for them during their
May 12, 1981

younger years, to learn the joy of building as opposed to whatever joy they get out of destroying.
The first item in this bill that appeals to me is that young persons should bear responsibility for the actions that they undertake. That has not been the case for a number of years. I remember a court case in the province of Alberta where a group of young people between the ages of 12 to 15 broke into a hardware store, took the paint and the brushes and painted everything, in the store. They made a terrific mess. They dumped paint all over the floor and all over the other items. When they came before the magistrate, he slapped them lightly on the wrist and said, "Now, you should know better than that. Go home and don't do it any more." Who bore all the expense? The couple who were operating that store were not young. They were barely making a living. They had something like $3,000 worth of damage. They, who had nothing whatsoever to do with the crime, had to pay the total cost.
I said at that time, and 1 say it again, that the court did those young people no favour whatever in letting them get away with the "fun". If they had been told by the court to go back and clean up that mess, at least it would have taught them the lesson that they should not have done it. But they were not required to pay, they were not required to do anything except listen to a little lecture from the magistrate, and one of them said afterwards, "I wish he hadn't talked so long. I wanted to go somewhere else."
1 think we have to instil in our young people the message that if they destroy, they must pay, if they cause damage to somebody else's property, they must pay. I cannot say it nearly as well as the hon. member who just sat down. If we do not do that, we encourage young people to continue a life of crime. That is what some of our laws and courts have been doing inadvertently, not deliberately.
I know of another case where a group of young teenagers, all under the age of 16, thought it was fun to remove a "bridge out" sign on a district road. They moved the "bridge out" sign and they burned it. That night a young married couple, who were, as a matter of fact, on their honeymoon, went along that road and, of course, there was no "bridge out" sign. They went into the ravine and both were killed. Someone said to me, "Those young people will feel remorse the rest of their lives." I do not know whether that type of remorse is worth it or will bring back any happiness to the loved ones of the couple who were killed inadvertently because someone committed a thoughtless act and destroyed a sign.
I want to emphasize that this entire act should be predicated upon the fact that we pay for our sins, and if we destroy someone else's property, we pay for it in one way or another. That brings me to the second point I want to make. The juvenile courts have been working hard to help young people. Do you know how many times some of these young people have appeared in the courts? Would you say five or ten? When a juvenile judge asked me, I said, "Six, seven." He said, "Would you believe it? The boy you saw in court today has been before this court 55 times." That boy laughs at the court.
Young Offenders Act
The court could not do anything except levy a fine which his parents glibly paid. They had lots of money.
That is the point I think my hon. friend from British Columbia was just making. That is encouraging a boy to be a criminal. He loses his respect for the courts. In this bill, at least, I see a number of items now which will permit the courts to be effective so that they will no longer become a laughing stock among those who apparently want to be criminals. It will certainly restore the dignity of the courts and will give our juvenile judges some authority and some options that they can use in dealing with this matter.
The next point I want to deal with is the causes. Why do young people get more fun out of destroying rather than building? Why do young people want to steal rather than earn their money? Why is it that two young boys may live in the same neighbourhood, in the same environment, yet one goes out and works after school and on Saturdays to make his money while the other one steals it? I think we have to analyse the reasons for the criminal act, for the misbehaviour, or whatever you want to call it.
I would like to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and continue this evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before continuing I would like to take this opportunity to welcome the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) into the House. We missed him badly this afternoon; it is nice to see him here this evening.
In my view the cornerstone of this bill should be to build human lives into something worth while, to take a piece of broken earthenware and make it into a vessel of substance, to make good citizens out of those who somehow or other got on the wrong track and, to put it in a nutshell, to encourage our youth to build, not to destroy.
Before adjourning this afternoon I was endeavouring to deal with some of the causes of youth offences. This bill should play a very important part in encouraging analysis of those young people who are starting off on a life of crime. When we talk about rehabilitation, there is no better time to start it than in their young years. We should not wait until people are 40, 50 or 60 years old and then try to use our prisons as centres of rehabilitation. When we try to analyse the causes of young people becoming offenders and coming into conflict with the law, it is impossible to say in a blanket manner what causes persons to go down the wrong path. Tonight I would like to suggest a few causes I have found in dealing with young people. If one finds the cause, then one has a much better

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
chance to rehabilitate and to correct whatever is causing the difficulty.
One cause which I have found to be very high on the list was learning disabilities in school. For many, many years we did not realize that slow learners had a problem. As I heard some teachers say, we thought they were dumb or dull. I have heard some people say that they lacked initiative. But when one really gets down to the root cause and finds a slow learner, when one finds that a young person is not keeping up with his class, generally there is a very sound reason. Some people do not learn as rapidly as others. Boys and girls who go through school like to be thought well of by their peers. As a student and as a teacher, I found that analysing boys and girls to discover why they were not keeping up with their class work was an important job. When 1 found the cause, then generally I was able to help the young person. Sometimes I found they were simply slow learners; it was just as simple as that. They could not keep up with the regular lessons. I remember asking one boy who was having difficulty in grade five or six when I taught in a country school of 11 grades, "How come, John, you cannot keep up?" He said, "Well, I do not understand what you are saying." I said, "Why didn't you say so?" "I do not like the other kids to think I am dumb", he said. So I said to him, "How would you like to stay in for half an hour a couple of days a week after your classmates leave and we will go over the things that are bothering you?" "Oh, boy," he said, "that would be wonderful." By the time that lad reached grade 12, he was one of the top students in the school. We found out what the trouble was-John was a slow learner.
1 went through a correctional institution in Edmonton a few years ago and I checked the number of students who were there. It was my belief that at least 40 per cent of those yong people who had come into conflict with the law and who were in that institution were there because they either had a learning disability or were slow learners and they had never been diagnosed as such, or ever helped. The school system had failed those people. As a matter of fact, I saw a boy 14 years of age in that correctional institution with a book in front of him. I saw from the cover of the book that it was a detective story. I thought it strange that he should be reading a story of that kind during classroom hours. When I walked to the back of the room I saw that he was reading a grade three reader. He had covered the book with the jacket from a detective story so that he would not feel bad. He had never learned to read. It is no wonder that by the time he reached grade five or six people called him dull. He was not able to keep up with the other students in his class. He had not learned the fundamentals in grades one, two, three and four, so he became a drop-out. Then his only friends were those in a similar category who came into conflict with the law. That boy said he did not want to break the law but the only friends he had were criminals. All of this was because he was a slow learner, because the educational system had failed him.
I would ask the Solicitor General to inquire into the number of young people in our prisons who are there because they were
slow learners or who had a learning disability and who came into conflict with the law, not because they wanted to but because the school system had not taken the trouble to find out what was holding them back.
In the correctional institution in North Edmonton they were going right back to the grass roots. Boys from 14 to 17 years of age were learning how to read. Once they had learned how to read, a whole new world was opened up to them. One boy of 18 said to me that he had not realized before that it was so simple. He reached grade seven and he still could not read, so he dropped out of school.
I think we must analyse the reasons why people become criminals. Sometimes our system forces them into this way of life. As the hon. member from British Columbia who spoke before me outlined, it is sometimes due to parental attitudes. Most parents like to see their children do well; but many parents do not realize whether their children are slow learners, fast learners or somewhere in between. Some parents do not realize that their child has a hearing or sight disability which can hold him back to the point at which he can no longer catch up with his peers, so he becomes an outcast and he finds other friends.
A policeman in Edmonton told me about finding a 13-year-old girl on the streets of Edmonton at one o'clock in the morning. He asked her what she was doing there. She had no answer. He found out where she lived and he took her home. The girl's parents were asleep. After rousing them, the policeman said to the girl's father, "I found your daughter down on Jasper Avenue at one o'clock this morning." The father was angry and asked the policeman why he had not left his daughter there. "Why are you waking us up in the middle of the night?" he said. That kind of parent is making criminals out of his children. The policeman said that he felt terrible as a result of the father's response. He said that he was only trying to help the child but even her parents did not seem to care.
Perhaps the reason that some of our young people lose direction is that they have no home life to speak of, no father or mother to encourage them to do the right thing. They drift off to the only place where they can find some friendship. I think some of these children just make a mistake. I am sure every hon. member in the House can think back to the time when he was a youth-a time when we all make mistakes. If we had been picked up by the police every time we made a mistake and charged with a criminal offence in a court of law, maybe we would be in a penitentiary today instead of in the House of Commons. There are excellent people in our penitentiaries today who are there because of circumstances, because they made a mistake and everyone thought they were criminals.
Sometimes our police do not help matters either. I forwarded a letter to the Solicitor General recently about a group of excellent young people who were being hounded by police officers who thought they were doing their duty. I remember a boy who came to my boys' camp one year about whom my assistant said to me, "I don't think we should take this lad." I said to him, "Will the boy be having a holiday?" My assist-
May 12, 1981

ant's reply was negative. I said, "Then we are taking him in. That is what the camp is for." When the boy got to camp I took him into my tent and said to him, "Bob, I am sure glad I have you in my tent." Bobby said, "You are?" I said, "I sure am!" By the end of the week that boy was an excellent camper.
1 said to him, "How come you are always getting into trouble in your town?" He said, "Every time someone breaks into a store or breaks a window, the police come to my house. What is the use of me trying to be good?" He said, "Out here people treat me well. That is why I did not break any rules. I do not like breaking rules, but 1 have been hounded by the police." I believe police officers are taking steps today to ensure that this type of situation does not happen. It is a responsibility they have. Because a boy makes one mistake is no reason for him to spend the rest of his life as a criminal.
Then there are the ones who decide, through laziness or something else, that they will spend their lives as criminals. They decide that they will get rich by stealing, they will take what other people earn. These are the most difficult people to deal with. They have made up their minds to pursue a life of crime. I think there must be a penalty imposed on these people so they will know that when they break a rule, they will be punished.
The next point I wish to make deals with restitution. I wish to congratulate the present Solicitor General and the former solicitor general for providing a number of alternatives to our courts for dealing with almost every type of youth who comes into conflict with the law. Restitution is one of the most effective measures provided. This afternoon I cited the case of young people who broke into a hardware store and threw paint all over the place. They received a slap on the wrist and were told to be good. Within the month some of those boys had taken a truck and run it through a wall. The court had done them no good by telling them that it would overlook the first offence because of their youth. As I said before, we do our young people no good whatsoever when they commit a crime like that if we simply say, "Don't do it again." In the first instance, the magistrate ordered the boys to go back and clean up the paint. If they had worked there for two or three days before this happened, I do not think they would have driven that truck through the wall. They should have had to rebuild that wall.
There are many ways of obtaining restitution, and it is one of the best ways of making people realize what they have done. 1 heard of a case in Edmonton a few years ago, of a young man from a large eastern city who had never seen a pig. One day when a policeman was going by, he called him a pig. He followed the policeman around, calling him a pig. Finally the policeman arrested that 16 or 17-year-old lad. He was tried in court and the magistrate asked him if he had ever seen a pig. He said he had seen pictures of them but had never seen a real one. The magistrate sentenced him to work on a pig farm in north Edmonton for one week and said that when the boy came back he would consider what to do then. The boy worked on the pig farm, and when he returned he told the magistrate
Young Offenders Act
that he would never call anyone a pig again. He had learned his lesson. Had he simply been given a fine, which his father might have paid, he would probably still be calling policeman pigs, and perhaps worse.
Restitution is an excellent thing. Most of us learned at home that when we did something wrong, we had to pay the price. We learned that we either had to take the punishment that was coming or make good the damage.
I grew up with a boy who broke a fence one time. He simply decided to tear down the fence. We did not go to court about it, but his father said that he must rebuild the fence. I went along with him, because I was with him when he did it, and I helped him build it just as good as it was before. Today that lad is a minister of the church. He knew that if he did something wrong, he would be punished.
I hope that through this bill we can make people realize that if they do something wrong, they will be punished. Let us have no bleeding hearts about that point, which is a very important one.
When the court decides to send an offender to an institution, we should be sure that it is an institution where they can learn to build and not to destroy. 1 had occasion to visit a young lad who was convicted of killing his stepfather because he had committed a heinous crime against the boy's sister. He was just over 16 at the time. I went to visit him in a federal penitentiary. I asked him how he was getting on, and he said, "I am learning how to become a criminal." I asked if the guards were not counteracting that. He said, "No, you are with the prisoners all the time. I have learned more about crime in the time that I have been in this institution than I ever dreamed I could. I do not want to be a criminal but they are making me a criminal." I was happy when he left that institution and I hope he is doing well now. He was not a criminal type. He had made a mistake and maybe there was some reason for that. But he was not learning much in that institution, except about crime.
In many of our prisons today there is idleness and no work. That is one of the reasons why many young people get into trouble today. They have nothing to do. I had plenty to do when I was growing up. I had to rush home from school every night during the winter months to haul coal or to chop wood in the summer. There was always lots to do. I envied the boys in the cities who had nothing to do. I do not envy them now, I feel sorry for them. If they had lived on a farm they would always have had something to do. The devil finds something for idle hands to do, which is not good.
We should provide the opportunity to inmates of our penitentiaries or correctional institutions to learn how to work. We should give them something worth while to do.
That is one point in favour of the Bowden Institution which the federal government now operates. Some time ago a boy came out of there who is now operating his own tinsmithing shop. He learned to be a tinsmith in the institution. Before that, he had no trade, nothing to live for. Now he is a good

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
citizen, is married, and doing well in his business. The objective is to try to rehabilitate these people.
As one hon. member remarked earlier, the cornerstone of this bill should be to encourage young offenders to build, to turn from their criminal activities and become not only good citizens, but to learn how to enjoy life. They should learn how to attain happiness from helping others, not robbing them; they should learn how to attain happiness from helping others less fortunate, rather than trying to tear down lives that have been built up, or stealing from others. The cornerstone of this bill should be to build, not to destroy.
