speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a day of information for members of the House regarding juveniles in our society. It has been a day characterized by concern shown by members of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada in this House who have demonstrated throughout the debate their concern for the young people of Canada, as they have done in the past.
It has also been a day of surprises. Of the 282 members of the House, 147 sit on the Liberal benches. It would seem that those 147 have no interest in juveniles because the day has been characterized by an absence of speakers from that side. 1 wonder if they have lost interest because we are dealing with a population that does not vote. I find that so much of the government legislation that comes along is dedicated not to wisdom and not necessarily to what is good for all Canadians, but perhaps far too often is characterized by what might be seen as something positive in the way of garnering votes. I am particularly pleased that the sponsor of the bill, the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan), saw fit to attend for perhaps 20 minutes of the debate this evening. He was not present this afternoon and currently is not in the House. I hope he will come from behind the curtain or some back room and listen to our concerns about the legislation he has placed before us this evening.
I should like to remind hon. members who were not present earlier that we are currently debating an amendment to the motion of the Solicitor General. The amendment is proposed by a former solicitor general, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), and is seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), members of the Conservative party. The amendment states very clearly and very succinctly that it is the opinion of those members of the House that this bill should not even go forward to committee for further study because in its basic principles, it is based on inequality. 1 should like to read that amendment so that we are all clear on what we are debating. The amendment reads:
That this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-61, an act respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, because the bill rejects the fundamental principle of equal treatment of all persons before the law by specifying that the act will apply to different age groups in different provinces.
I find it somewhat surprising that an 88-page bill would be brought before this House after the months of debate we had on the Constitution of Canada. It violates what we have been told is one of the principles of the Liberal Party of Canada, which is the current governing party of Canada, that all Canadians everywhere in Canada should be treated equally. Perhaps that should not be surprising. The last day we sat in this chamber was April 23. That evening we voted on the Constitution of Canada. The government party opposite, aided and abetted by the New Democratic Party of Canada, and its members from Saskatchewan, voted in this House to say that all of us in western Canada, as a consequence of the votes on that Thursday evening, would have less protection in the Constitution of Canada than we had before those votes.
The people who live in Quebec and in Ontario, through their elected officials, have a veto on future constitutional change. They are entitled in perpetuity to the protection of the Canadian Constitution. Prior to that vote on April 23, those of us who live in provinces in western Canada could, under certain circumstances, combine with one other province to exercise the veto. We did not each have a veto in each of the four western provinces but one province could combine with one other province. Two provinces acting together could protect themselves from unwanted constitutional change. But on the night of April 23, the governing Liberal party, aided and abetted by the New Democratic Party, said that was too good, "we want you weaker than that." From that moment on, no one premier in western Canada could veto constitutional change to protect us from changes we do not want. Not even two premiers could do that. It will take three premiers from western Canada to equal one premier from the province of Ontario or one premier from the province of Quebec.
Then I look at the bill before us tonight. I have been sitting is this chamber all day wondering whether or not debating this bill is a waste of time. I am glad to see the Solicitor General has come back into the House for a few moments. He appeared before the constitutional committee. During those hearings we tried to find out what was going to happen when the new Constitution was brought in. I want to bring one clause of the Constitution to the attention of hon. members. It is clause 15(1). It reads:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law withouth discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
I wish to emphasize the word "age" in that clause. Here I have before me an 88-page bill which says with crystal clarity that, depending on your age, you will not have equality before and under the law. I think a case can be made that a three-year-old requires a different response from society than perhaps even a six-year-old, and certainly somewhat different than that required for a sixteen-year-old.
1 find in this bill the concept of "your" protection, and I say to all of the young people-although I suspect very few are watching our proceedings on television this evening-that this government has brought forward a bill which states clearly that if you are 17 years of age, you will have a certain
May 12, 1981

protection under the law in some provinces, in other provinces if you are 16 you will have that protection, and in still other provinces, if you are 15 years of age that protection will be afforded to you. Therefore, depending on where you live in this country, under the young offenders act, which will be a federal law, young people will be treated differently by the law.
I say to the young people, those perhaps who would like to break the law, that if this becomes the law in Canada and a person happens to live in Hull, he or she might be better off if that person came across the river to Ottawa. Likewise, if a person lives in Ottawa, the law might treat that person better if he or she crosses the river and goes to Hull. How does that jibe with the glowing statements we have heard in the last few months about the concern of Liberal party members for the rights and the equality of Canadians? We do not get it in terms of constitutional amendments as we lump ourselves together in provinces. We do not get it in terms of basic law as it affects the young people in this country. The government wants it different. Depending on the province in which a young person lives, he or she will be treated differently by the courts of Canada based on his or her age.
At the same time, I wonder whether it is all a giant public relations hoax because the majority opposite will force this Constitution on the country, if it possibly can. Does the government think that this act will be struck down because it violates the basic principles inherent in what has been called a charter of rights and freedoms? Then where will we be in this country if this particular act is, all of a sudden, declared illegal by the Supreme Court of Canada? Where will we be in terms of our ability as a nation to treat the young offenders of this country? That should give cause for concern to all members of this House who come here charged with the responsibility of making this a better nation and a better world for all of our people.
Why do we deliberately proceed to discuss an 88-page bill, to move it to committee, to call witnesses and to spend all of that time on a piece of legislation which may be declared ultra vires? If the Solicitor General were here and if he were in the mood, I would ask him-although I probably would not get an answer because I am a member of the opposition party- whether he has taken the trouble to submit this bill to justice department officials for a legal opinion on whether or not it will be ultra vires of the Constitution of Canada, assuming that the new Constitution were in place. I can guess that he has not done this. The reason I guess that is that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) himself, on many occasions in testimony before the constitutional committee, has said, "we will worry about the legislation which is on the books of this country, we will examine it for its legality, not before we pass the new Constitution, but after."
The provincial government of Quebec has paid some very skilled legal talent to examine legislation which exists in that province. These people were to advise the Quebec government on what would happen to legislation if the new Constitution were put in place. It was reported that at least 100 pieces of legislation would become illegal instantly. We have a federal
Young Offenders Act
government which seems determined to use its transitory majority to change this nation in a hurry in ways which will be unalterable in the future. The least we could have would be a statement from the Solicitor General that he has a solid legal opinion that this legislation, if passed in conjunction with the proposed Constitution act of 1981 will still be declared legal. If there is any probability, and I suggest there is, that it will be declared illegal, why should we in this House spend today, possibly tomorrow, and who knows how many more days in the House and in committee, examining a piece of legislation which will be declared by the Supreme Court of Canada to be beyond the competence of Parliament?
Through the Constitution act, 1981, we are saying that the Supreme Court, five out of nine judges chosen by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or a particular prime minister of the day, without public examination, will be able to tell the Parliament of Canada, the duly elected people of this country, what they can legislate and what they cannot. That is the fundamental revolution that will take place. I suggest it has an impact on this piece of legislation.
Before we debate this much longer, I ask the Solicitor General to tell us clearly and unequivocally whether he has sought and obtained a legal opinion on whether this legislation will be declared ultra vires of the Constitution act, 1981. If he is not prepared to do that, I suggest to the government House leader that there would be considerable wisdom in arranging for this House of Commons a different order of business until that legal opinion has been sought. There is not much point spending the time of the members of this House and the tax dollars of Canadians debating a piece of legislation which is very likely to be declared ultra vires.
Any piece of legislation which takes us into the area of criminal law deserves more careful examination by the duly elected members of the House of Commons than most other pieces of legislation because it speaks of society's determination to protect itself. At the same time it speaks of society's determination to use its collective power to deprive individuals of their freedom. For those of us who have reached this point in our lives without having run afoul of the law or being charged with any criminal offence, this may seem to be distant. However, we all read in the newspapers from time to time about a miscarriage of justice where an individual has been charged, convicted and sentenced for a crime he or she did not commit.
We have an obligation to move slowly and carefully on the specifics of such a piece of legislation because we are trying to balance two very difficult principles at the same time: the protection of society from the wilful and damaging acts of an individual or groups of individuals, and at the same time the protection of the kinds of freedoms on which all of us in a society like ours place great value.
With the passage of time, our society has adopted a third principle dealing with rehabilitation. There is a concern for whoever is charged with breaking our laws and damaging our

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
society. We treat them in a manner calculated with the best wisdom we have to ensure they do not repeat that offence. The process of involving them with our police and judiciary is calculated to produce a situation where people change from violating our group mores or standards to making a positive contribution. That is an important third element in our system.
As I read this bill, I find a fair amount of creativity, which runs counter to our historic patterns in the Juvenile Deliquents Act, which will be helpful in meeting the goal of rehabilitation. A number of members have spoken about restitution. For example, if a young offender has broken the law by defacing a building, the likelihood of his continuing that kind of pattern might be reduced if he is forced into a situation where he has to clean the building, carrying out the hard physical labour in order to put it back to the state in which he found it. Research evidence shows that kind of sentencing and treatment has a positive effect. Some parts of this bill will make that kind of treatment more likely and, therefore, recidivism less likely.
1 am bothered about the other two aspects: protection of society and protection of the individual. This is not the proper time or place to deal with the bill in its entirety. We cannot in a speech in the House of Commons deal with the specifics of an 88-page bill. The purpose of a second reading debate is to deal with the bill's principles.
The first principle identified in our amendment which I find bothersome is that the bill clearly specifies that Canadians who live in different provinces will be treated differently under the law. That is unacceptable. Whether you live in Newfoundland, Quebec or Alberta, a federal court comes under federal jurisdiction. All Canadians should be treated equally and not differently depending on the province in which they live. On the basis of that fundamental principle, this legislation should be rejected until that principle is attended to and brought back for our consideration.
I know that time is running along, but I would like to deal with two or three other issues in clause 3, the declaration of principle. I wish to quote clause 3(6):
Young persons who commit offences require supervision, discipline and control, but, because of their state of dependency and level of development and maturity, they also have special needs and require guidance and assistance;
Where is the empirical, scientific justification for that statement of principle? Which 17-year-old youngsters require supervision, all those who break the law? What positive consequence is inherent in the concept of supervision? What do we mean by that? In societal terms it means parole officers. Historically that has been our method of supervision. Has it worked? I suggest the scientific evidence would indicate that supervision is not necessarily the answer for all these young offenders. Do they all need discipline and control? Are they all in a state of dependence?
I have just returned from a visit to some other cultures and societies in the last couple of weeks where I observed first-hand 15 and 16-year-olds who were in the work force in apprenticeship programs. On the basis of my observation I would say
their maturity and lack of dependence was a great deal greater than some of the 30-year-olds 1 have run into in my lifetime.
Surely the guiding principle involved here is that we as a society when we encounter young offenders should operate on the principle that we study the individual case, the particular age and the particular state of maturity of that individual and then attempt to design as well as we can a set of circumstances which will assist that individual in avoiding the commission of an offence in the future.
When we include a principle such as this, I wonder whether it will be possible for lawyers to argue in a court of law that particular decisions taken run counter to the principle of the proposed young offenders act. I also wonder why we have clause 3(c) which reads as follows:
Where it is not inconsistent with the protection of society, measures other than judicial proceedings under this act should be considered for dealing with young persons who have committed offences;
I wonder why we have judicial proceedings. As I sat on the committee on the Constitution I remember spending some days on the legal rights portion of that proposed measure. Those of us who are not lawyers, I think, all found it educational.
There are protections that come from a judicial system which do not come from other kinds of systems. I wonder why we are to have a principle in this proposed act which sort of invites the setting aside of judicial principle, and I wonder whether that will be used too frequently to the detriment of the young people who come under the law according to this bill we are considering tonight.
Clause 3(d) states:
Young persons have rights and freedoms in their own right-
I wonder, after trying to go through the bill, where those special rights and freedoms are to be found. 1 can remember testimony, again before the committee on the Constitution, by those involved in the Year of the Child, members of committees from across this country, who said that if we are to have a bill of rights, we need a section which deals with children and young people. I know, standing here this evening in this House of Commons, that there is no such section.
I see in this bill a statement of the principle that because of age and the state of maturity there need to be special rights. It even says that young persons have special rights and freedoms, but I cannot find them in this bill and 1 suspect they should be there.
I could go on in detail about other clauses in this bill, but in the last two or three parts of the statement of principles we encounter the concept of the family, and we encounter, in a very minimal sort of way, the concept of parenthood. If the Solicitor General were to heed the wisdom of members of the Conservative party in this House and withdraw the bill for changes, I wonder if he would spend a little more time in developing a stronger section about both the rights of families in Canadian society and their responsibilities.
Certainly when we proposed that the whole concept of the family and its importance in our way of doing things be part of
May 12, 1981

the Canadian Constitution, that concept was rejected by the New Democratic Party and by the Liberal party. They do not believe that the family has any place in the Constitution of Canada. If they are not willing to have that concept of family enshrined in the Constitution of Canada and they do not think it is important in that measure, perhaps at least they could deal with it in a little stronger way in relation to the importance of the family and parents to young offenders and their relationship to young offenders. I suggest to the Solicitor General, members of cabinet and, hopefully, to the odd backbencher who might somehow get the courage to stand up and speak on this bill, that they consider strengthening that portion of this measure, and draw perhaps a somewhat clearer line, not just about the rights of families and the rights of parenting, but the obligations of families and parents. They have certainly specified with some degree of clarity the right of state over the rights of the individual. Perhaps they could balance it a little bit by strengthening the clauses dealing with the issues I have just mentioned.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I once again reiterate the fact that members of our party, the former solicitor general of Canada being the mover, have recommended that this House not give this bill second reading and reference to the committee. In effect, we are inviting the Solicitor General to withdraw it for more work. The reason for that recommendation is that the bill does not recognize the fundamental principle that all Canadians should be treated equally under the law. This is an 88-page bill deliberately dedicated to the production of inequality under the law. Therefore, in principle it is unsound, unCanadian and should be withdrawn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin tonight by commending the minister for bringing this measure forward. In doing so, I think he has indicated both respect and sincerity in his intent. I think it is important legislation to Canada and Canada's young people today.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) correctly identified the objectives and purposes of this measure when he stated in the opening that:
They must strike a balance between helping young offenders and protecting society from harmful conduct. They must safeguard the rights of young people in conflict with the law, while discouraging offenders from committing further crimes.
I think that is fairly well stated. If I were to change one thing in those objectives, it is the tone which I find throughout Canadian law; we always talk in the third person instead of in the first person. We always talk about what "they" must do. I would like to see the word "they" corrected in an attitudinal sense to say instead "we" must strike a balance and "we" must safeguard because we must take that "we" even beyond ourselves as legislators and look at it as "we" the legislators, "we" the parents, "we" the community and "we" Canadians, not just the great "they" as in "other people" or some professional "they" who will solve our problems with juveniles.
Young Offenders Act
In his conclusion, the Solicitor General says:
It is the various professionals, such as family and youth court judges, lawyers, police officers, welfare officers and social workers who are responsible to make the system work.
The Solicitor General is wrong here. The age of specialization in which the professional has all the answers-just give him the problem, and it will be solved-is over. That has not worked. Our statistics show that. The professionals do not have all the answers. That has not worked.
The Solicitor General is responsible to make it work, not the professionals. Not only is the Solicitor General responsible, but I am also responsible. I am responsible to make it work. All members of the Canadian community are responsible to make it work, and there should be that emphasis that it is about time all of us took our responsibility instead of trying to pass off responsibility for juvenile delinquency or adolescent delinquency. Instead, we should say we will all take our responsibility when and where we find it.
Not only do we refer to the great "they" in referring to those who will solve our problems, but we also refer to the other "they" all too often. The second great "they" is the juvenile offenders. No longer will a juvenile offender be an offender when we accept the great "they" offenders back as part of all of us, because that is where they came from. They came from the "we", the "us" sector, and they became the "they". They became the rejections from our homes, from our schools and from our communities and, most important of all, they became the rejections from their peer groupings, a most important factor among young people of this age. We need to recognize that it is not just they who have needs. The great "they" have the same needs we have. We, like they, all need acceptance and acknowledgement through positive achievement. We need open and honest relationships. We need correction without overcorrection. We need respect and love.
Who are the great "theys" we are talking about here tonight? Who are these "theys", these juvenile delinquents? Let us identify them a little more closely. Before this act is passed, the offenders are those between 7 and 18 years of age. After we pass this act, we are talking only about a small part of that child-adult grouping, and I refer specifically now to 12 to 17-year-olds. That is narrowing it to a very particular group called adolescents. We are now talking about adolescent offenders.
Who and where are these adolescent offenders? We can even narrow it a little more than that. Statistics show that the offenders to whom we refer specifically within that 12 to 17-year-old grouping are 14 and 15 years old. Fifty-six per cent of juvenile or adolescent crime is committed by 14 and 15-year-olds specifically. We can narrow that even further and find that the peak among young men is in the fifteenth year. Eighty-six per cent of offences are committed by young men. The stereotype or prototype is specifically a 15-year-old male. Why do 14 and 15-year-olds get into so much trouble?

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
Before I came here tonight I posed the very same question to the 14 and 15-year-olds in my house. I asked my daughter Jill and my son Kiven and their two friends, Glenn and Stewart, why 14 and 15-year-olds get into so much trouble. Their answers were indeed very revealing. In fact, I think they are the answers as to why young people get into trouble. They said young people get into trouble because they lack attention. They said young people get into trouble to try to gain some acceptance. They said they get into trouble because of family breakdowns and family problems and because they want to follow in their friends' footsteps. Their friends are doing it, so they want to do it too. They do it just for kicks or to add some excitement to their lives. They do it to be "cool". Above all they must be cool. They do it because they are bored. In a society which has given them everything, they are bored. There is a lack of direction. I think these young people have very well identified why young people get into trouble.
I spoke with a judge from the United States about this bill. He gave me some interesting statistics. He said that one of the problems he is facing is the family break-up situation. He said that in the state of Oregon where he is a judge, 81 per cent of marriages end in divorce. That is four out of five marriages. He gave another interesting statistic about family relationships as the basic problem, or one of the basic problems, causing adolescents to be brought before the law. He went around to the prisons to which he had sentenced young people and did a personal survey upon which he calculated statistics. He asked two questions. The first question he asked those young people was, "Who do you care about in your family and who do you think might care about you?" It was interesting that 82 per cent responded that either mother or sister loved or cared. The next question was, "Who do you hate in your family"? Ninety per cent said they hated their fathers. I only point this out to indicate the importance of the family structure, and that family structure has to be taken into account in any rehabilitative or corrective format because it is here that we have the greatest possibility for correction, for rehabilitation, and for reacceptance. We can perhaps reaccept a young person into a group home or a foster home, we can perhaps reaccept a young person into the school or into some community sports organization, but the ultimate success will depend on whether we can rehabilitate and get reacceptance by the family of that child. That is a critical area in any rehabilitation or reform.
Again, we can sit and list all the reasons why young people get into trouble. We all want to blame or list. We keep blaming. How many times have 1 heard the cycle of blame? Parents point their fingers at the teachers in the schools and say it is the teachers of the schools; and the teachers in the schools point the finger right back home. The police often say, "Why arrest them? The courts just release them on to the streets again, anyway." The courts say, "We do not make the law," and they blame the politicians; and the politicians blame everyone else. It is not a matter of blaming. It is, instead, a matter of accepting the responsibility and beginning to do something about it. I hope that this bill is the beginning of
acceptance of responsibility, and starting to point toward a program and policies which will work back toward acceptance and acknowledgement of young people through positive achievement.
I speak on this subject, not lightly, but with some experience, because, as a schoolteacher, I was given a group of 25 young people and told, "Do what you will with them. They are failures. They are 13 to 15. They are in Grade 8. They are not going anywhere." Some were slow, some had emotional problems, some were just cowering and frightened. But I did find, in working with these young people, everywhere I went, that they had one thing in common. They were all rejects. They were rejected by every element of our society.
If we are going to just reject them, they are going to react; and they will not accept rejection. They will fight that and they will gain acknowledgement. They will gain acceptance one way or another, and the only way that is open to them is negative because the positive ways have, in fact, been closed to them. Those routes have been closed. Many hon. members who have teenaged children can watch this rejection by the schools and by the society. It happens at 14. It happens at 15. Young people are suddenly confronted with the reality that a door is closing. We must end that rejection and turn it into reacceptance and reintegration.
We need to establish community service programs and restitution agreements. We need a sense of responsibility. 1 again refer to a section of the Solicitor General's report. He promises that this program is going to develop and that this act, policy or legislation will somehow provide community service programs and restitution agreements. He recognizes that the courts have worked in this direction and that by doing this we will establish a sense of responsibility, and opportunity to repay, and self-respect and self-esteem. Reacceptance amongst peers, schools, community and family are also factors which will have to be included.
When I was a member of the legislature, in the first year that I was elected I travelled to all of the correctional institutions in the province of British Columbia. I read about an idea called "youth juries". This was an idea of getting peer group interaction. The youth jury, in fact, would sit and judge with their peers and then perhaps call for community restitution. Then, following community restitution, hopefully this same peer group of young people would reaccept or take some responsibility to bring the young person back into their group. The kinsmen group or the Kiwanis, or whatever, would run some night programs, sports programs, and things like this, to try to find an opportunity for young people to achieve and to gain some recognition, following which they would move back into the schools and into the community.
As a result of representations, such an experiment was tried in my community. It really worked quite well to a point where it broke down in that people were not willing to carry it through. They would go as far as setting up the court and making the judgments, but they would not carry through on the reacceptance back into the community. However, this
May 12, 1981

youth jury idea was tried in British Columbia and I think it has been tried elsewhere.
I think the idea of community service programs, restitution, accountability, are important factors, and I am glad to see that there will be some flexibility in the program to carry out these kinds of experiments. That is, in fact, what they are: experiments. But we need to experiment because we need alternatives in our programs. We cannot really blame the judge if he has only two or three choices. If all he can do is sentence the young person to jail or release him, we cannot expect the court action, the rehabilitation, to have much effect, because just to release a person or just to send him to jail is not the answer and does not provide enough alternatives.
We need alternatives which include strengthening our foster families and homes. We can do that federally. We can say that it is the provincial government, but it is not necessarily the provincial government. There is a substantial number of tax incentives which might get people from other areas, other families, and other types of families interested. There are incentives which could be provided to perhaps produce more and stronger family groupings. We need group homes and we need community support groups. I will be interested to see what the minister has to say about these kinds of programs, for which, he says in his booklet here, the federal government takes responsibility.
There are some specific concerns about this bill which I do want to mention. I do have concern relating to youth court records. It is fine to say that the court record will be destroyed; but in this day and age of modern science the court record is only one small part of the record of that young person. The more blatant and difficult one is found in computer records, because a young person can be picked up, charged, fingerprinted and photographed, if he is to be treated like an adult, and only then the charge is dropped. But the information, just that he was charged and the charge was dropped, is still in the computer, a computer whose access and interconnection is highly questionable in today's era of public information.
So my concern is that when we are talking about records, we are not just talking about court records, we are not just talking about a criminal record filed here in Ottawa. We are talking about all records, including interconnected computer records which relate not only to charges which were followed through, but, in fact, all charges which relate to young people who may have been accused wrongly or may have been treated unfairly by an unfair conviction which has been followed through.
As far as public hearings are concerned, one of the good things about youth juries, it was said, was that if there was public understanding, part of the punishment and rehabilitation was, in fact, a form of guilt, public humiliation and shame. That is what this part of the legislation implies; this open public hearing concept somehow implies public punishment. I am not sure it is what we want for two reasons. The first reason is that when we talk about a 14 or 15-year-old adolescent who will be reaccepted in the community, the reacceptance is made too difficult by punishing him publicly,
Young Offenders Act
by holding him up to ridicule and exposure. It may not work; I urge caution.
On the other side of the coin, many young people seeking negative attention commit crimes for attention. When he is punished in public, he kind of likes it because he gets a lot of attention. I am concerned about these public hearings or these court hearings. When these hearings are held in private, there is a better opportunity for rehabilitation than when public ridicule and scorn is heaped on a 15-year-old. They will get it any way; they will get it in school and they will get it in the community. To play with it in the newspapers and to play with it in public by letting people sit in who are not involved needs rethinking.
As far as fingerprints and photographs are concerned, I would have very grave concern if my child were picked up by the police for whatever reason, taken to the police station, charged rightly or wrongly, fingerprinted and photographed. Parental responsibility is accepted when the juvenile is taken in, certainly there should be a protection whereby no fingerprints or photographs are taken without parental consent and knowledge.
An hon. Member; It is absent in the bill.

It is absent in the bill. It indicates that we will treat them like adults. We must break it down right to our own children. Somehow when we talk about "they", we talk about someone else's child. But when we legislate we must legislate for everyone's child as well as our own. We must take that into consideration. I hope someone is listening. Whoever that is, I ask them to reconsider the section on fingerprints and photographs.
Another section which gives me concern is the one on flexible sentencing, that somehow we will make it more uniform or more rigid. I am not sure that is correct. Surely the objective is to rehabilitate and return a 15-year-old to society. We must have the maximum flexibility to judge that young person as he matures. This ties in with the difficulty of putting a maximum age on determining whether a person is a juvenile. The 14, 15, 16, and 17-year-old grouping is a difficult one. Which child is an adult? Is it the child who has survived out in the world by himself for two years? Is he more responsible than a child coming from a highly protected home who is physically and mentally immature or somewhat physically and mentally slow? When does one become a mature adult? I wish we could see, on this upper maximum age, some way to determine whether a child is a child, whether or not he is responsible. We should almost leave that to the judgment of the courts. I know it cannot be done, I know the flexibility is not there. It is moving toward rigidity, and I am concerned about moving toward rigidity.
At page 19 of this bill it is indicated that the Government of Canada is responsible for programs developed to meet young offenders' needs. I want to be very clear about this because usually we hear governments saying that they are not respon-

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
sible. It is hard to define responsibility, but the federal government has committed itself to programs in this bill. That must be the meat of this legislation.
It is nice to tidy up things, but in fact the programs developed to meet the needs of young offenders are the test. The minister's ability to define the needs and the programs of young offenders will be the measure that determines whether or not this bill represents a significant step, as the minister indicated in his response. The significance is found in the one sentence to which I have referred. I challenge the minister to define that significance for us.
There are many things this bill will not do. This bill will not change the economic conditions of inflation and high interest which forces two parents to carry on two full-time jobs, or perhaps three, just to survive or meet their basic requirements of food and shelter. It will not change the social disadvantage of economic privation; it will not change that. This bill will not solve youth unemployment, nor will it solve the social and negative results of the drug and alcohol symptoms of the turned-off youth in our society. It will not solve those problems. The attitudes of this bill must be a larger part of every piece of legislation which passes the House of Commons. We should not be discussing only the effects of adolescent crime at this time. When we are discussing inflation and high interest rates, we should be reminded that there is a relationship to youth problems. When we are discussing a bill of rights in the House of Commons, we should be recognizing the value of the family relationship. I am disappointed that we did not recognize the importance of the family in our Constitution. The family must be made strong so that young people, the adolescents about whom we are talking, can find a way back into their families. We need to show our intention, that we understand it by mentioning it in our Constitution. We need to recognize that materialistic values must be redefined or reunderstood. Perhaps it is more important to have a little less materially but to have one parent in the home. It is important to have a father in the home. There is an attitude in society that we all go out to work in the morning and we come home to rest. When we come to rest, our family is there, our young people are there. It should be the other way around. We should go out to get a job, to earn a living in order to build our families, and we should come home to work with our young people and to spend time with them. What a hypocrite I am to stand here at 9.30 at night saying that we should spend more time with our families. I stand on the floor of the House on my son's birthday. My wife had to go out to a PTA meeting-and here I am. We must begin to work with our families in order to strengthen them, to strengthen our values and to uphold those which are right and sound. They are the value of the family, our spiritual values, our societal values, the values of work, achievement and recognition and acknowledgement of those achievements, and the heritage of our country. All these values must be upheld in everything we do in this House of Commons and in the way in which we live.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we speak about this bill, it sometimes seems that it is not of too much significance. Surely if we look at it carefully we will see that it is, in fact, the very core. It is where we see reflected all the things which are wrong with our society, in the abuses and neglect which we show to our young people. I think we can create this 15-year-old boy that we are talking about now. This 15-year-old boy needs a time and a place, a time to achieve and a time to be recognized. Can we create that society? Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to address a matter that really should have been dealt with a long time before I was elected to this House. Although I am thankful for the opportunity to take part in this debate, it seems to me that the opportunity should not have been accorded due to the fact that this piece of legislation should have been introduced and passed many years ago. Yet, I must express my surprise at the Solicitor General's comments as to the amount of discussion which should be afforded to this bill by the members of this chamber. When he introduced this bill for second reading on April 15 of this year, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) said:
-I think a relatively short period of time should be devoted to second reading-
Obviously, his reason for making that suggestion is so that the bill may proceed to committee where full discussion should take place. I believe this is a bill of great importance, not only to the people of my constituency but to the entire population of Canada. Therefore I hope that the Solicitor General will forgive me for delaying somewhat the referral of this bill to committee in order that I may let my views be heard in this chamber.
As I have already stated, this legislation is long overdue. As the Solicitor General indicated in his remarks on April 15, there have been many previous ministers responsible who have made an attempt to introduce such legislation. Undoubtedly the Solicitor General's predecessor, the hon. member for Dur-ham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), would have done so himself had it not been for the fact that the Liberal government, in co-operation with the New Democratic Party, decided to change the direction of Canada and push us all down an economic spout and defeat the previous administration. No doubt the present Solicitor General has been itching for an opportunity to introduce this bill for quite a while, but he has not had the opportunity to do so due to his leader's preoccupation with the Constitution and getting it through Parliament.
When I say that this bill is long overdue, I have in mind the comments of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) when he was solicitor general. On December 18, 1974, as reported on page 2363 of Hansard, the then solicitor general, in response to a question from my colleague, the Conservative member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), said:
We hope to have a draft bill and a white paper prepared for early spring.
Unfortunately, the House never saw that draft. It did not see a draft in the spring of 1975 or in the spring of 1976. Finally, in the spring of 1977 a sort of draft bill was intro-

May 12, 1981
duced by the then solicitor general, who now sits as the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox). On March 21, 1977, the then solicitor general introduced a paper entitled "Highlights of the Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders." Many of the members on this side of the House, such as the former member for Calgary North, Mr. Eldon Woolliams, were great proponents of the young offenders legislation. They believed that the time had finally come. A week after that paper was tabled, a series of meetings began between federal and provincial representatives to hammer out the consensus needed to ensure that the enactment of such legislation would, in fact, meet the desired goals. But that proposal did not quite get to see the light of day.
It can be seen that as far back as 1967, when a bill was brought before this House dealing with the antiquated star chamber attitude of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, right up to the present time we have discussed in this place over and over the fact that the present act should be changed.
I sincerely hope that this bill will not meet the same fate as previous ones. We can see why the Solicitor General might be a bit worried and why he might suggest that we get on with it and refer this matter to committee. Generally, we on this side of the House can agree with him. We understand the need to accomplish the passage of this legislation. But we still believe that this bill is not perfect. Yet it is still a good piece of legislation. This is certainly not surprising in light of the fact that the present Solicitor General had the hard work and expertise of his predecessor to draw from, along with many other solicitors general from previous years. I do not mean to take anything away from the present Solicitor General in saying that.
I would now like to turn to the contents of the bill which, as I have stated, has many substantive changes within its pages which are badly needed. In Bill C-61 we see that the over-all philosophy has shifted from one of parental responsibility in the Juvenile Delinquents Act to the more acceptable and practical approach of a youth being held responsible to some degree for his actions. This is the same philosophy which was adopted by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland when he was solicitor general. It is also the same approach as put forward by the ministerial proposals of 1977. This is described in section 3(1) of the bill which states:
It is hereby recognized and declared that
(a)	while young persons should not in all instances be held accountable in the same manner or suffer the same consequences for their behaviour as adults, young persons who commit offences should nonetheless bear responsibility for their contraventions and society must be afforded the necessary protection from illegal behaviour;
At the same time this bill addresses the adult, which I think is significant and very important. Section 10 (3) states:
A parent who is ordered to attend a youth court pursuant to subsection (I) and who fails without reasonable excuse, the proof of which lies on that parent, to comply with the order
(a)	is guilty of contempt of court;
(b)	may be dealt with summarily by the court; and
(c)	is liable to the punishment provided for in the Criminal Code-
Young Offenders Act
We can see that the bill begins to address the responsibility of the young person, as well as the responsibility of the adult.
There is no problem for members on this side with the minimum age under which a youth may be prosecuted under the act. As we all know, the present statute holds that a seven-year-old can be prosecuted. The bill before us changes the minimum age to 12 years old. The limit of 12 years is certainly a reasonable one and one which has found agreement on all sides of the House, as well as in the provinces. However, where we do get into difficulty is where the maximum age is concerned. This is due to provincial inconsistencies. It was the desire of my party to have a uniform maximum age, that age being one on which both the federal and provincial governments could come to an agreement. That was our position, and it is still my hope, Mr. Speaker, that this government can garner an agreement from the provinces in order that such uniformity can be achieved. This is the entire reason for the amendment put forward by my colleagues, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland and the hon. member for Edmonton-Stratchcona (Mr. Kilgour).
I would also like to draw attention to the legal and other rights which will be granted to young offenders through this legislation. Such rights are a necessity for this to be a meaningful piece of legislation. I am glad that they are included.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on at length about the good points of this bill, for there are many. However, I feel that there are other aspects that should be mentioned at some point in this debate, aspects which are not really touched on in the bill and which could therefore easily go unnoticed, both in this chamber and at the committee stage.
What I would like to speak to now are the rehabilitative aspects of the bill. It has been said many times in this House that our greatest resource in this country is not our oil and gas, nor is it our forests and fisheries. Our greatest resource is neither a vegetable nor a mineral. It is our children. That is where our future lies. With that in mind it should be clear that a good deal of emphasis should be placed on the future path of our children. This bill certainly goes a long way in improving the prospects of delinquents, but we must ask if it goes far enough.
Surely one of the reasons we have had a separate piece of legislation for offenders against the law who are not adults is that we desire to make sure that the young offender does not mature into an adult offender.
We can look at this bill and see that the legislation does attempt to ensure that a life of crime will not continue. This is evident when we look at the dispositions available at the court upon conviction. They range from an absolute discharge to such things as a $1,000 fine; restitution and compensation orders; getting the offender involved in community service; having the offender compensate the victim; probationary periods of up to two years; custody of up to two years; ancillary conditions, and combinations of all of these.

May 12, 1981
Young Offenders Act
I was very fortunate when I attended college in Minnesota that the professor of one of my classes was the head of Minnesota corrections. In dealing with him and working with him I was very fortunate to have an opportunity to work on a movie on the juvenile institutions of Minnesota.
One of the things brought out in that work very clearly and profoundly was the need for more than just institutions. We saw the whole gamut, from the bars and unbreakable glass right through to the pretty colours, plexiglass and nice looking buildings, but in fact that is not where the answer lies.
What really worries me is that not enough will be done to ensure that an offender will not return to his or her old ways. I am hopeful that this topic will see much discussion in the committee stage, and I hope that such discussions will not be limited to just the items which are covered by the bill. For example, I point to the rapid rate at which juvenile offences are accelerating in the middle-class strata. Not long ago there were many who believed that the rate of juvenile delinquency was a problem only in poverty-stricken homes. I do believe that is the case, Mr. Speaker. In fact, Mr. Marc Leblanc not long ago conducted a study to determine whether delinquency, defined as law-violating behaviour, is distributed randomly throughout the various economic strata. He states as follows:
-It is interesting to note that the adolescent from the upper class milieu commits as many delinquent acts as the adolescent from the working class milieu.
He continues and concludes:
Economic development and a rise in the standard of living do not seem to reduce delinquency. Poverty and posterity alike seem to produce the same effect.
In his essay entitled "Middle Class Delinquency", Mr. Leblanc also states:
-Observation indicates that the highest rate of delinquency exists in the most affluent countries.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, our problem does not stem from the economic situation; it comes from something more serious, more rooted, something to which we must give more thought.
One of the things that society and we as individuals must address is the whole matter of the divorce rate, and stress on the family. What is happening? Our family unit is breaking down. The divorce rate is climbing. Is it any wonder that those kids lack a responsible adult model to follow? Does that in itself not create a lot of problems that result in an increase in juvenile delinquency?
If it is not an economic problem, then we should be looking at other areas, not only as legislators but as individuals and family people ourselves.
I am trying to point out that as an affluent nation, we can expect to have an increase in juvenile offences as our level of affluence rises. This means that we will have more and more children who will have to be watched through the legislation which is before us today. It means that the young offenders' court system will have a greater burden to carry in the future. Yet, nowhere do I see any indication that the facilities will be provided to ensure that the young offender will have the opportunity to be rehabilitiated before it is too late.
In the same context, I should like to point to another danger. This has to do with the provisions in the bill for commital and custody. We see that the youth court will retain jurisdiction over the offender until the sentence is pronounced, at which time the provincial director will decide on the place and level of custody. It is extremely crucial to have adequate facilities available for young offenders where they will not be exposed to criminal methods.
If a province is unable to handle its young offenders, that is, if a province is unable to provide an institution where a youth offender is placed in a hospitable surrounding, where will that offender be placed? What kind of institution will that young man or woman be sent to? If we look at the reform schools which presently house many of the offenders under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, we can see that they are certainly not the type of places that are totally conducive to reform. Albeit the facilities are certainly better now than they were 20 or 30 years ago, I find it hard to believe that they are good for the offender.
As stated in the principle of the bill, society must be protected. We must ask ourselves: at what cost should society protect itself? Should we begin to upgrade and improve the youth detainment facilities across the country, or should we be content with the present facilities and cross our fingers in the hope that the 14-year-old B and E artist will somehow see the light through the barred windows of his reformatory dorm?
As I mentioned earlier, when studying in Minnesota I had an opportunity to study a novel experiment being carried out in Europe which had some merit and which I think we should be examining in Canada. A widow in a community would be given a very small home and a small group of juvenile delinquents. She would also be given a very small amount of financial assistance, just enough to allow the group to feed and clothe themselves. It left them with a certain amount of financial need. As a result, those kids were expected to contribute to the financial needs of the home. The impact was phenomenal and the results were tremendous. The recidivism amongst those kids was almost zero.
In his essay, "Learning Technical Skills", Peter Letkemen gives a detailed account of the effects of reform institutions on the young offender. Mr. Letkemen points out that in most cases a person does not commit crime as an adult after a period of normal middle-class life, but that early delinquency "does seem to be a prerequisite for the adult criminal career".
Mr. Letkemen shows through numerous case studies how the hardened con began his career by stealing hub caps for which he was sentenced to a period of correctional rehabilitation in a reform school or similar institution. Time and again the cases show that in most instances the offender was actually educated in those institutions on how to become a successful criminal; hence the title that Mr. Letkemen uses, "Learning Technical Skills" is really a tongue-in-cheek title. In fact, those technical skills are criminal skills, skills that we do not want our young people to learn, skills that we are trying to do away with. In fact, the institution is a university for that kind of learning program.
May 12, 1981

I should like to read a few passages from this work which illustrate what I am trying to say. He writes:
Delinquency is also associated with the reformatory experience, which seems to be a first formal step in the direction of the criminal career.
Not only does it segregate the delinquent from his non-delinquent peers, but reformatory conversation as my respondent's comments indicate, centres around crime, perhaps even more than in jails and penitentiaries.
In other words, the point of interest for any debate seems to be crime. Mr. Letkemen goes into an actual conversation he had with one of his cases, as follows:
He mentions that he worked in a factory for three years and did part-time stealing on the side. He started using drugs and was arrested for illegal possession of narcotics and sentenced to six months in a reformatory, and in there he felt his criminal education began.
The convict then says:
And I went to a reformatory and in there I would say my criminal education began. In the shop that I was working at, that is, in the reformatory, I got talking to one guy about laying notes. And he showed me a couple of ways of laying notes, and explained to me how lucrative it could be. And various other ways of B and E-
We can see that in many cases reformatories are nothing more than educational institutions, promoting an education and giving a degree in something that our society and our legislation is trying to eradicate.
Perhaps those remarks would be more suitable in a debate on penitentiary reform. But I want to point out to this House that this is a very difficult aspect of the revision of the antiquated Juvenile Delinquents Act. It is important to bear in mind that the protection of society from a juvenile offender is obviously in society's interests, but it is even more obviously important to ensure that the juvenile does not become an adult offender. One of the things I discovered in working on a movie in Minnesota was that the recidivism rate among juveniles was 63 per cent. That means, for every 100 young people who ended up in some kind of reformatory, 63 would return. Obviously that system is not working. What are we going to do in Canada? We have to address that problem. It is a fundamental element of this bill.
This legislation before us does much to improve our old ways. The dispositions of the court are many and varied in order that the judge may find the best method of protection and rehabilitation. The committal to and the release from custody portions of this legislation are certainly better than those we have presently. The review of dispositions will certainly go a long way in keeping a watchful eye over the offender. But I ask this House to place some emphasis on the fact that we must protect the young offender from the world of crime if we are to protect ourselves. I hope that when this bill reaches committee, members from all sides will look for ways in which this legislation might be improved in this area. For the thousands upon thousands of young people who know not what they are doing, we should explore this area meticulously before we enact this bill.
I mentioned briefly the amendment put forward by my colleagues. It is an important amendment. If I can refer very
Young Offenders Act
briefly to the bill, I think we can see why. If we look at clause 2 under the heading "Interpretation", we can see the definition of an adult. An adult means a person who is neither a young person nor a child. If we turn to the next page we can see "young person". The definition reads:
"young person'' means a person who is or, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, appears to be
(a)	twelve years of age or more, but
(b)	under eighteen years of age or, in a province in respect of which a proclamation has been issued under subsection (2), under sixteen or seventeen years, whichever age is specified by the proclamation,
and, where the context requires, includes any person who is charged under this act with having committed an offence while he was a young person or is found guilty of an offence under this act;
If we look at those two definitions, we find right off the bat that we have started off with an inconsistency. We have a problem. In one province a person is an adult at the age of 16 while in another province a person is an adult at the age of 18. In one province a person is still a kid at the age of 17, while in another province at age 16 the person is an adult.
The amendment which my colleagues have brought forward is one that I can support wholeheartedly. I think it is a great improvement to this bill. As I have said throughout my speech, there are many things that I find good about the bill, many things I can support, and I think when we look at this amendment and attach it to the bill, we will find that we are dealing with and improving a piece of legislation which is so necessary. This is very important legislation. It affects our real assets, our youth. It is a far-reaching bill with many implications. It has many things which all of us must be concerned about as parents, as members of society and as legislators. It is important. Therefore, I would like to conclude tonight by saying that I would encourage the Solicitor General to support my colleagues' amendment so we can see this legislation proceed and begin to address some of the problems we face in society today.

subtopic: WESTERN DEVELOPMENT FUND-IMPROVEMENT OF INSUFFICIENT WATER SUPPLIES
WESTERN DEVELOPMENT FUND-IMPROVEMENT OF INSUFFICIENT WATER SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reference that I am about to discuss tonight goes back to last February 26, page 7700 of Hansard. On that occasion I had addressed a question to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that was prompted by his speech to the Montreal Canadian Club on February 23.
In that speech the minister made a direct reference to the $4 billion western development fund, $2 billion of which was to be spent over the next three years as a catalyst for co-operative efforts with the government and people of western Canada to ensure that potential constraints to longer-term development such as, and this is a direct quote from that Montreal speech, "inadequate transportation services or insufficient water supplies, are addressed on a timely effective basis."
I then asked the minister to enlarge somewhat on that very specific reference to insufficient water supplies in the west. I am sure that my question, which was a very serious one, caught the minister off guard as he was only able to respond very generally and vaguely.
In my supplemental question, I was even more specific and asked if this water reference might relate to a much-needed long-range contingency drought policy which the west is dearly in need of, or could it refer to the challenge of interbasin water transfers from rivers in northern Canada to southern Canada, in the west.
1 also made a sincere and appropriate compliment about that high profile federal agency, the PFRA. I sincerely hope that the parliamentary secretary who is to respond does indeed address himself to my remarks and obvious concerns about prairie water supplies and the serious potential of drought across the southern prairies.
Since last February, the potential for another drought has worsened considerably, and I say that in spite of the first general rains of the spring that came only last week. Those rains were quite adequate along western Alberta, but tapered off to much less than adequate at the Alberta-Saskatchewan border. In my opinion there is sufficient soil moisture to start growth in both our grasslands and cultivated soils. This is an improvement over last year. However, the critical feature of this potential drought situation is the serious shortage of surface water across the southern parts of all three prairies provinces, and this for the second year in a row.
I am referring to an almost total absence of snow run-off water over that entire area. This, of course, was the inevitable result of no snow to melt in the spring, a situation which began on Christmas day and really developed into a winter drought for the balance of the entire winter. The net result was a complete lack of a spring flood for the thousands of small forage projects which produce most of the forage feed supplies for next winter, again for the second year in succession.
It is the western cattle industry that will once again face severe feed shortages, and this time with considerably less carry-over of hay from previous years as well as reduced grass
May 12, 1981

supplies. I must point out that spring and early summer rains can still come-I certainly hope they will-but, with very few exceptions, they will not make a hay crop.
The minister's Montreal speech sounded as if the government had some contingency plans for needed water development on the prairies. If this is so, why not tell us about it? If PFRA is to be given the green light on a new phase of water conservation and utilization, let us hear about it. We have already had six weeks of serious dust storms from Lethbridge to Dauphin, Manitoba.
In spite of all of our present-day sophisticated weather techniques, there is no reason why we cannot have another decade of drought like the dirty thirties of 50 years ago. Let us take another look at interbasin river transfers in the west from our northern streams to the Saskatchewan-Nelson basin system, but all in Canada. The time may not be too far off when our freshwater supplies will be more important than our diminishing petroleum supplies. I have already said the western cattle industry will bear the brunt of this potential drought, much more so than the prairie grain industry.
Is it not about time for the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to support the cattlemen's income averaging trust account proposal? This is a carefully researched plan put forward initially by the cattlemen themselves with the support of many associations and provinces. It essentially provides for a beef cattle stabilization plan on an individual cattle producer basis. It has much to commend it. This is the type of year when that approach could be very helpful.
My main remarks tonight are directed to the reference of the Minister of Finance to water in that $4-billion contingency plan for the west. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: WESTERN DEVELOPMENT FUND-IMPROVEMENT OF INSUFFICIENT WATER SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the hon. member in the absence and on behalf of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion who left for Europe this evening. In order to give him some particulars on the point he brought up in his question of February 26 with regard to insufficient water supplies and the possibility of a federal program, that is, a program providing emergency assistance in case of drought and the participation in such a program of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration.

The constraint of adequate water supplies in the prairie region of western Canada applies to economic activity in all sectors, not only farming, from basic resource processing to agriculture and community and industrial development. The drought periods are those periods where inadequate supply shows up, and the very nature of the drought and when it occurs often has different effects on the economy. Recent analysis shows that a drought affecting agriculture in Saskatchewan by reducing, as an example, farm income to the
Adjournment Debate
extent of $450 million, could have a negative over-all effect on the Canadian economy of $1.6 billion.
With the increase of economic activity in western Canada, it is time to define these water constraints in relation to economic growth and stabilization-and in this I agree with the hon. member-to determine the level of water supplies which are adequate in times of drought, and to implement projects and programs to release these constraints.
The federal government, of course, does not operate in the water supply field unilaterally. The provinces have extensive responsibilities in respect of water management and economic development. Therefore, discussions with the people of western Canada and provincial governments particularly, must be a prelude to the federal government implementing programs to release water constraints.
It is, therefore, too early to say at this time which projects could be selected and what role the PFRA could play in the planning and implementation of those projects. It is not too early, however, to say that water supplies offer extensive constraints to economic development, and the federal government is willing to play its role in relieving these constraints.
In respect of the general planning and development of western Canada from the source of that $4 billion, perhaps the basic thing is to tackle this first problem before spending more money, making sure that everyone is protected; not just the farmers but those people who will help the further economic development of western Canada.

subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-I. RESULTS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL DISCUSSIONS-APPEAL FOR RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTS. 2. FUTURE OF CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT
AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-I. RESULTS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL DISCUSSIONS-APPEAL FOR RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTS. 2. FUTURE OF CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks this evening stem specifically from my questions in this House on Monday, April 13, 1981, regarding the ailing auto industry in this country, and generally from many other questions during the last year to date put by me, by other members of this House, and certainly by the ladies and gentlemen of the press and others concerned with the state of the auto industry, which not only affects its employees and the industry itself but the economy as a whole.
I will not dwell on statistics because of time limitations and because basically most people know the statistics in this area. However, I would like to bring those statistics up to date very quickly. Yesterday the Automobile Importers of Canada came out with a statistic which shows that one out of every four cars in this country is an imported car. That is an increase of 71.5 per cent over last year. The second statistic shows that the Canadian deficit on parts under the U.S.-Canada auto pact has reached a staggering $4.2 billion. Those two areas, imports and the U.S.-Canada auto pact, are the two major concerns this government should be facing. Indeed, for over a year the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and others from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce

May 12, 1981
A cljournment Debate
have had numerous discussions and consultations both with the United States, with regard to the auto pact, and with offshore exporter countries, particularly Japan, which now sells 21 per cent of all automobiles sold in Canada.
When asked about the auto pact, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said, "We are not talking about joint decisions", that is, with the United States; "we are talking about making our own decisions". That was on April 11 or 12 of this year. However, no decisions have been taken. There have been none whatsoever. When we asked him about imports after the Japanese made an agreement with the United States, he said we will take unilateral action if the Japanese do not give us terms similar to those they gave to the United States. The discussions of last Saturday between the Prime Minister of Japan and our own Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have failed. In fact, there are reports today that an official of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce said:
We have had a telex from our trade mission saying there was progress made on both sides during the talks. There was agreement to hold further talks-
That is the progress being made.
In the few minutes I have left I want to point out two things. First, Japanese imports must be curtailed to some extent, and not just with quotas because our situation in Canada is different from the situation in the United States. Therefore, we must not only legislate quotas but we must also tie them into an increase in local content plus an increase in foreign investment in the auto industry in Canada. We need this because after the agreement between Japan and the United States to reduce Japanese imports into the United States by 7.7 per cent, Canada is virtually alone among western industrialized nations with no restrictions whatsoever except the conventional duty. I could go down the list. Australia, the United Kingdom, France, Argentina, Italy and Spain all have restrictions dealing either with local content or other forms of restrictions which support their own auto industries. Yet in our country that industry is going down the tube. This affects one out of six employees in Ontario alone.
The second point upon which I want to touch is anti-dumping by the Japanese, and by the Soviets as well with respect to their Lada cars.
I have dug up statistics with respect to specific Japanese models. The Honda Civic, for example, is sold in Canada for $769 less than it is sold in the United States. The Datsun 310 is sold for $828 less in Canada than it is in the United States. The Toyota Tercel is sold in Canada for $721 less than in the United States. That is, of course, before federal sales tax and the exchange of the dollar is taken into account. However, the Japanese receive roughly 18 per cent to 20 per cent less for the same automobiles which are dumped into Canada, and this is before the reduction in the United States. Can hon. members imagine what will happen to our market if members of this government continue to sit on their fat behinds and fail to act, except to talk and to say there will be more discussions and more discussions? What will happen after imports into the United States are reduced? Hundreds of thousands of cars suddenly will not be shipped into the United States. They
cannot be shipped to the other western nations because they have restrictions.
I will refer to just one example. In Mexico there is 50 per cent local content. An imported automobile has to have 50 per cent local content. The list goes on.
I realize that I am running out of time. I do not want the parliamentary secretary to say the same thing the minister has been saying, that is, that there are more deliberations and meetings under way, because the industry, the economy and we have had enough. It is time this government took some action, and now is the time to take the action. I want to hear what it will be and when it will be taken.
