subtopic: HEALTH AND SAFETY-USE OF DALKON SHIELD INTRAUTERINE DEVICES
HEALTH AND SAFETY-USE OF DALKON SHIELD INTRAUTERINE DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1971 some 127,000 Daikon shield intrauterine devices have been sold in Canada. The manner in which this device entered the Canadian market, the inadequate premarket testing of this device, the inadequate substance and application of our medical devices regulations, and the continuing inaction of the Liberal government which has endangered the health of Canadian women, illustrate precisely the type of situation that in Canada has become the rule rather than the exception.
Since becoming NDP health critic, I have asked many questions in the House relating to medical devices. None so completely exposes the weaknesses of our medical devices regulations as this one concerning Daikon shields. None so completely exposes the fact that Liberal governments are only willing to act after large numbers of complaints are received by the Department of National Health and Welfare about a particular device.
A little history is in order. As I said before, some 127,000 Daikon shield intrauterine devices were sold in Canada prior to 1974. Ninety per cent of these were actually implanted in the bodies of Canadian women. In 1974, A. H. Robins, the manufacturer of this particular device, ceased production presumably in an attempt to stave off the perceptions of liability which were growing with the evidence that more than 20 per cent of women who had Daikon shields had problems within three years of insertion. This is U.S. data, as usual there is no Canadian data.
Adjournment Debate
These devices were not recalled by government. Women were not informed of the danger. The company simply stopped making them. Subsequent studies showed that if a shield is left in for seven years, the probability of a major problem occurring is almost a certainty.
In September, 1980, A. H. Robins, responding to the growing body of literature associating the Daikon shield with a certain form of pelvic infection, put out a press release concurring with recommendations that the shield be removed from asymptomatic women, which is to say, women who as yet are experiencing no problem with their Daikon IUD.
The problem is this. According to Robert Manchester, a lawyer for the Boston Women's Network and an expert on the issue, there are likely some 12,000 women in Canada who may still be using this device.
All I have asked of the government in the House and subsequently in a letter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is that a medical alert be put out on this device. Why not? What is the reason for not doing so?
In a letter of reply to me, the minister said that there have not been enough Canadian incidences to justify any action. How many is enough? Does the minister think that the reproductive organs of American women are more susceptible to disease than those of Canadian women, thus invalidating the evidence? By what twisted logic or, worse, fatuous indifference characteristic of the Minister of National Health and Welfare does she purport to be acting responsibly in this particular situation?
In its response to me this evening, no doubt the government will lament the fact that there are thousands of classes of medical devices on the market, and bewail its incapacity to test or regulate them all. What it will not say is that only five classes of these devices out of those thousands are subject to regulation and premarket review, and these five have been picked in response to public opinion rather than systematic scientific caution.
We are the laughing stock of the western industrialized world when it comes to the protection we offer Canadians in this area of concern, that of medical devices. If the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not act soon on this by bringing in amendments to the appropriate legislation and in other ways so that Canadian women and their health are not sacrificed to profit and to the inertia of her bureaucracy, she will be quite rightly laughed out of her image as protector of the health of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: HEALTH AND SAFETY-USE OF DALKON SHIELD INTRAUTERINE DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the intrauterine device marketed under the trade name Daikon shield was manufactured by A. H. Robins of Richmond, Virginia, U.S.A. It was first available in Canada in August, 1971. It was promoted actively and its sales here rose from 26,000 in the first year to 54,000 in 1973. By 1975 a total of 127,000 units had been distributed.

May 12, 1981
Adjournment Debate
The company became aware of some 36 cases of septic abortion in the U.S.A. in 1973 and, in consultation with the health protection branch of the Department of Health and Welfare, issued a "Dear Doctor" letter on May 30, 1974, informing Canadian physicians about potential problems. At about the same time, further sales of the device were suspended in Canada. A survey by the department's regional offices that fall confirmed that the Daikon shield was no longer available for sale on the Canadian market.
In view of the importance of intrauterine devices, a nationwide survey was carried out in 1974 to determine use patterns and adverse reactions. The evidence obtained via questionnaires from physicians did not indicate that the Daikon shield was significantly more hazardous than others. However, it became evident that IUDs in general could give rise to health problems, and all major manufacturers of this product were asked to submit before March 1, 1975, evidence of safety and effectiveness of their IUDs. On June 4, 1975, the Canadian distributor of A. H. Robins was informed that, on the basis of evidence submitted, further sales of the Daikon shield would be considered a violation of the Food and Drugs Act. Other manufacturers were requested to provide a package insert
listing pertinent warnings and directions for the benefit of the patient. At the same time, steps were taken to require premarket review of all future IUDs.
Mr. Speaker, in 1975, there was no firm scientific or medical evidence to justify replacement of implanted Daikon shields. However, more recent data indicates that there may be increased risk of pelvic infection if the residence period of any IUD is extended beyond three years.
IUDs, then, have been subject to premarket review since 1976, and manufacturers are now required to recommend explanation or replacement within two years. This matter was reviewed by the health protection branch advisory committee on medical devices only yesterday, May 11, 1981. The contents of a possible "alert letter" to physicians are under discussion. This would review the recent literature and refer to recommended times of removal for each type of IUD.
